speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: TEXT OF PROPOSAL TO BE CONSIDERED FOR SIGNATURE IN WASHINGTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to lay on the table of the house the text, in French and English, of a document which I trust will become of historic importance. It is the proposal for a North Atlantic treaty which is to be considered and, if found acceptable, signed in Washington during the first week of April. Copies are available for hon. members, but for greater convenience I would ask that it be printed also as an appendix to Hansard of today so that it may be available to all those who receive Hansard and get their documentary information from its pages.
At the same time I would call attention to notice of a resolution appearing on page iii of the Votes and Proceedings of yesterday. Hon. members will see from the recitals of that resolution that a conference is to be held in Washington early in April for the purpose of completing such a treaty among the states named; and it is hoped that the situation in parliament will permit a brief discussion of this resolution before the date fixed for this meeting in Washington, so that the sense of the house may be obtained. I should hope it would be the sense of the house that Canada should be represented at this conference in Washington and continue to put forth its best endeavours to bring about the signature of the pact along the lines of this proposal.
(For text of proposed North Atlantic treaty, see Appendix, page 1671.)

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The house resumed from Thursday, March 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. Abbott that the house go into committee on the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a measure to provide for the continuance in force of the Foreign Exchange Control Act until sixty days after the commencement of the first session of parliament commencing in the year 1951.
Motion agreed to, and the house went into committee, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it will be possible to deal with the various sections of this bill at a later stage in the procedure, but in the meantime it is important to consider some of the principles involved and some of the points that have been made in connection with this proposal.
The bill before the committee is to replace a bill introduced some time ago to meet special circumstances. It is interesting to note the extent to which a bill of this kind, once it is on the statute books, is accepted by people who forget the considerations that were in their minds at the time the bill first came to their attention.
Since this law was originally placed on the statute book, many circumstances have changed and many things have served to emphasize the need for careful consideration of what has taken place. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) discussed this bill yesterday but made little reference to some of the most important considerations which have arisen since the first bill became law. The theory of foreign exchange control was one which the Minister of Finance himself indicated he accepted reluctantly at the time that step was taken. At that time, however, he contended that in view of the Bretton Woods agreement and our position in relation to the international arrangements then assumed, it was essential that we have this measure of control. Time passed and it was

necessary to review the circumstances in the light of what had happened.
In the foreign exchange control bill as it was originally introduced in this house there was an extremely important provision, under which pounds sterling were to be convertible with the dollar. For Canada that was a vital consideration at that time. Our difficulties in international trading are not with the United States, from the point of view of our monetary unit; our problem is to be able to sell in the sterling areas where in the past we have found our main export markets.
When the Minister of Finance speaks of exchange as being something which it is difficult to determine in realistic figures, he well knows that in the past the value of the Canadian dollar in relation to the monetary units of other countries was determined by the trade which Canada carried on in both dollar and sterling areas. The day by day value of our dollar was related to the possibility of converting our pound position into a dollar position in the ordinary exchange markets of the world. It is doubtful whether Canada would have entered into the Bretton Woods agreement and would have carried forward her undertakings without a further arrangement of some kind, had there not been reliance on the provision for convertibility between the pound sterling and the dollar of the United States.
When circumstances arose which led to the abandonment of the convertibility factor in the Bretton Woods agreement, immediately there was a reason for a review of the whole situation. As the Minister of Agriculture said in London not so long ago, and in forceful and vigorous terms, it is the duty of government to find some way in which the products of this country can be sold into markets which cannot buy unless there is some arrangement in regard to the sterling exchange. The whole situation has changed. Today we see a loss, and a threatened still greater loss in the future, in those sterling areas unless some mechanism can be devised for selling our products to countries to which we have sold them for so many years and which have been our largest export consumers. It is therefore essential that when the bill based on this resolution comes before us we understand that we are going forward without any indication by the government of any new steps which would assist the situation in which we find ourselves.
After all, the parliament of Canada must accept the responsibility of deciding whether we shall simply submit to a situation which exists or whether we shall take the initiative in seeking a solution to the problem posed by the Minister of Agriculture, who has felt 29087-102
Foreign Exchange Control the direct effects of this situation in dealing with the basic agricultural commodities of this country. When we are asked to carry forward the Foreign Exchange Control Act by the bill now before the committee, it is important to realize how necessary it is that the members of this house know perfectly clearly what the government intends to do, how these problems are to be solved, and how this country is to find an opportunity to extend its business in those markets which are now made difficult for us by the steps which have been taken under this act and through the failure of the convertibility factor in the Bretton Woods agreement. There is a special reason why this house should insist upon knowing what hope the government offer of some solution of that problem, and how they propose to deal with it.
We know what occurred after this act was originally passed. In the first place it was not intended that it should operate as a control over the exchange of goods between Canada and other countries. It was intended that this act should deal only with foreign exchange. When it was pointed out that this act went a great deal further than to deal only with foreign exchange, a reassurance was given that there was no intention of dealing with anything else. That is evident not only from the answers given by the minister, but also from answers given before the standing committee on banking and commerce by one of the representatives of the foreign exchange control board, who was put before that committee to explain the effects of this act.
In the reports of the standing committee on banking and commerce on Bill No. 195, foreign exchange control, as reported at page 40 of the proceedings of July 11, 1946, Mr. Rasminsky was answering certain questions in regard to the effect of this act and what the foreign exchange control board would do. These are Mr. Rasminsky's words as they are found in that report:
The foreign exchange control board has nothing whatever to do with the types or quantities of goods which are imported into Canada or exported from Canada.
On July 15, at page 53 of the report, Mr. Rasminsky was again being asked certain questions in regard to the effect of this act and the powers of the foreign exchange control board. These were his words:
The answer is that if circumstances arose in which for one reason or another it seems desirable to place restrictions on the import of goods into Canada then it is evidently the opinion of the government in this measure that the power to place those restrictions should not be conferred upon an administrative body such as the foreign exchange control board.
That is a clear and definite statement which, put forward in the way in which it
1608	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Foreign Exchange Control was, the members of this house have a right to accept as a guide in their understanding of the effect of this act and the operation of the foreign exchange control board.
On July 15 also, at page 57 of the report, we find that Mr. Rasminsky was asked this question:
Q. In other words, the suggestion there is no regulatory power vested in the board with reference to imports at the expense of any power parliament now has in that regard, Mr. Rasminsky, was referring to the export and import of goods rather than securities and currency? A. That is right.
On the basis of this statement it is quite clear that the impression was left that this was strictly a foreign exchange control bill and in no way dealt with the import or export of goods; yet we find that very situation has arisen.
Of course there were also the explanations given at the time that this matter was under discussion in the house. The then Minister of Finance is reported, at page 2547 of Hansard of Monday, June 17, 1946, to have made the following statements:
We have no intention of using this exchange control legislation to restrict anything but certain types of capital movement.
And later the same day, as reported on the same page, he said:
It is for this reason that it is necessary to maintain our over-all machinery of control, even though our intention is to place no restrictions on current account transactions.
The house had a right to rely on that assurance. I repeat the words:
We have no intention of using this exchange control legislation to restrict anything but certain types of capital movement.
Again we find that the present Minister of Finance said, as recorded on page 4530 of Hansard of August 9, 1946:
I repeat that the whole purpose of the measure is to provide for the efficient handling and conservation of our essential foreign exchange resources.
The word "whole" is not subject to any misunderstanding. It meant that the whole purpose, the only purpose, of this act was to provide for the efficient handling and conservation of our foreign exchange resources. It was at a later date that the announcement of a budget by radio, as described by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), changed the whole situation. At that time the present Minister of Finance made the naive statement that until they had been informed by the officials of the department they had no idea that the act contained the powers to do the things he was then announcing they were going to do. For a minister of the crown to say to the people of Canada: We had no idea that this act contained the powers we now exercise, but our officials have

informed us that we have these powers and therefore we shall use them, is simply a declaration by that minister that if any act is passed by this house containing powers that will enable them to do anything which in their use of arbitrary powers they want to do, they will do it, even though they had told the house they did not intend to do it. That, Mr. Chairman, goes much deeper than merely the accuracy of the statement of a minister of the crown; it goes to the question of good faith on the part of the government. It is inherent in our theory of responsible government that, when a minister of the crown gives an assurance with respect to government policy affecting the way in which the government will use an act that it asks the house and parliament to pass, the government will respect the undertaking which was given at that time.
Just think of what the effect of a disregard of that principle would be in relation to the other control measures which are now before the house, but which are not put forward by statute. If the assurance of the members of the government means nothing, as it meant nothing in this case, then assurances given that the government has no thought of using those powers in any particular way will also mean nothing. There is no other interpretation of the statement which was made by the Minister of Finance at that time.
But the minister went even further. He not only used the act to carry out the control over the import and export of goods, which he had said they did not intend to do, but he announced certain measures which could come into effect only when legislation was passed, and he gave instructions to the appropriate officials that they were to act on orders which had never received the authority or the power of parliament. That is simply government by dictatorship and not government by the parliamentary system. In the first place he repudiated the undertaking which had been given, and in the second place, having then used powers which they stated they were not going to use, he gave orders to departmental officials to carry out certain operations which were not even yet made possible by any act of this house.
When the Minister of Finance now treats in such a cavalier manner any criticism of the purpose or the operation of this act, it simply indicates how much he has forgotten the nature of the criticism which emanated from supporters of this government when this was done. Certain illuminating comments in regard to the effect of this act were made in the Senate, by men who had always been very close to this government. For instance, there was the comment of Senator McGeer

on August 13, 1946, as reported on page 680 of Hansard of that day. Amongst other things, he said-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: Order. Is the hon. member referring to debates in the Senate? I think it would be in order to refer to proceedings in committees of the Senate, but it is not usual in the House of Commons to refer to the debates of the Senate.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: Having regard to the practice in the house, Mr. Chairman, and having Hansard in front of me, probably I should have referred to "the other place". I would remind you, sir, that I am not referring to a debate in the current session, but to a debate which took place some years ago. I understood that these records of debates could be discussed from the point of view of interpreting the effect of a document.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: I do not think that the House of Commons has ever referred to debates in the Senate, whether they are debates of the current session or of previous sessions. The house has referred to other records of the Senate, but I do not recall the debates in the Senate having been referred to in this house.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: What rule is the chairman quoting? What is to prevent it?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: For my enlightenment, Mr. Chairman, I should like to know what rule prevents a reference in this house to a statement made in the Senate in relation to a bill which has become the law of Canada by the completed action of both the house and the Senate?

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: The only reason why the Senate was not quoted in this house before is that nobody over there had said anything.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
I have not the rule at hand, but my recollection is that if the house desires to know what the Senate has done, it passes an order to search the records of the Senate. I do not think any hon. member recalls a reference to the debates of the Senate, either of the current session or of a previous session, having been made in the House of Commons. The rule I had in mind was standing order 32:
This house doth consent that its journals may be searched by the Senate, in like manner as this house may, according to parliamentary usage, search the journals of the Senate.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, I do not think the standing order just read has anything to do with the question at issue. Surely what the leader of the opposition was reading from is now an historical fact, and these debates are open to quotation or otherwise in the house if members 29087-102J
Foreign Exchange Control see fit. There is nothing sacred about what happens in the Senate. It would not be proper for an hon. member to cast reflection upon what the present Senate is doing- although it may be a proper subject to reflect upon. I am sure, however, that in my time in the house a reference such as that which the leader of the opposition now seeks to make has not been forbidden by the rules of the house.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
I have been in and about the house a long time-about it more than in it,
I admit-but never until the last few days have I heard a chairman or a Speaker interrupt the leader of the government or the leader of the opposition.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: I am stating a fact. It is open to any hon. member to rise to a point of order. But until these last few days it has never come within my knowledge or observation that a Speaker or a chairman, of his own volition, has called a prime minister or a leader of the opposition to order. I should be interested to know whether this is a departure from the tradition that has been observed in the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
It is not my custom to interrupt when questions of procedure are under discussion, but I do see in Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, second edition, at page 95, citation 293 which reads as follows:
Besides the prohibitions contained in this standing order,-
That is, standing order 41.
-it has been sanctioned by usage both in England and in Canada, that a member, while speaking, must not:
(a)	refer to any debate of the same session on any question not then under discussion; nor
(b)	refer to any debate in the Senate, but he may refer to the official printed records of the upper house though they have not been formally communicated to the lower house.
The official printed record of the upper house is the minutes of the proceedings of the Senate, not Senate Hansard. I should be delighted, however, to hear what my late friend Gerry McGeer said at that time. I am not taking issue on that point at all.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
Order. I must agree that I was impressed by the remarks of the hon. member for Stanstead. It is only with the greatest of hesitancy that I would interrupt the leader of the opposition or any minister of the crown, and it has not been my custom to do so-although I think it has been done from time to time. The interruption I did make was in connection with referring to the debates of the Senate. As I had never heard it done in the house during the time I

Foreign Exchange Control
have been here, I thought it only proper that I should bring the matter to the attention of the committee. If it is to be the custom to refer to the debates of the Senate, then we should know. It would be an innovation, I am sure, so far as the House of Commons is concerned.
Standing order 41, to which the Minister of Finance referred, was the one to which I was about to refer. Citation 293 (b), in connection with standing order 41, states, as the minister has pointed out, that-
Besides the prohibitions contained in this standing order, it has been sanctioned by usage both in England and in Canada, that a member, while speaking, must not ...
(b) refer to any debate-
And I draw attention to the word "any".
-in the Senate.
It does not say, any debate of the present session or some other session; it is simply any debate. I take it to mean any debate of any session.
The rule to which I referred a moment ago was standing order 32. That is the one under which the House of Commons may ascertain what has been done in the Senate. I shall read it again:
This house doth consent that its journals may be searched by the Senate, in like manner as this house may, according to parliamentary usage, search the journals of the Senate.
That is the method the House of Commons has adopted of ascertaining what has been done in the Senate.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951

Mr. Chairman, I have no desire to _ press the matter, particularly from the point of view of considering, what was said. A question, however, has been raised which I believe should be settled with some clarity, now that it is before the committee of the whole house.
When you referred, sir, to citation 293, you read only as far as the words, "refer to any debate in the Senate". But the words which follow immediately after those words are these:
. . . but he may refer to the official printed records of the upper house though they have not been formally communicated to the lower house.

That refers to the minutes of proceedings of the Senate.
^ Mr. Drew: I know of the dispute which has taken place for some time in connection with the word "official" in that respect. The word "official" appears, of course, on Hansard, both of the House of Commons and of the other place. That is a matter which I suggest should be understood. I have another way of dealing with it, Mr. Chairman; I could [The Chairman.]

speechtext:
On the point of order, may I call the attention of the committee to citation 252 in the second edition of Beauchesne, which states:
The journals are the official records of the house.
It is a lengthy paragraph, but that is the gist of it. I confess when the point of order was first raised I was inclined to feel that it was being pressed too hard against the leader of the opposition. As I have been reading the citation, however, it has seemed to me that the chairman is right.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: To what citation is the hon. member referring?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
Citation 252 in the second edition, at page 76, which defines what are official records, and it states that "the journals are the official records of the house". Hansard is not an official record.
While I am on my feet may I draw your attention, sir, to another citation in connection with the point raised by the hon. member for Stanstead. The hon. member objected to the chairman of committees and the Speaker of the house raising points of order in the midst of speeches by the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition. May I quote in this connection citation 108 at page 33 of Beauchesne, second edition:
The Speaker decides the questions of order only when they actually arise and not in anticipation. He is bound to call attention immediately to any irregularity in debate or procedure and not to wait for the interposition of a member.
Surely the Leader of the Opposition and the Prime Minister are members of the House of Commons, with the rest of us, and subject to the same rules. I appeal to you, Mr. Chairman, not to have any reluctance to intervene in the speeches of the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition when, in your opinion, they are out of order.
One other point, lest the hon. member for Stanstead suggest that citation 108 refers only to the Speaker and not to the chairman. May I call his attention to citation 534 in Beau-chesne's third edition, which says, in effect, that committees of the whole house are, in actual fact, the house, and that therefore the same rules apply.

speechtext:

Foreign Exchange Control it deals with this particular point, and I am sure the Chairman will not find it to be contrary to the rules of the house. This editorial, which appeared on August 15,	1946, is
headed: "Liberalism revolts", and reads:
The government's bill to put in statute form the extraordinary powers of the foreign exchange control board received the reception it deserved when presented in the Senate. The senators' approach to what is beyond all doubt the most offensive and dangerous legislation sent over to them this session offers hope they will insist on retaining for parliament authority which a Liberal majority in the commons would have so meekly abdicated in favour of a bureaucracy of civil servants.
In preliminary examination the senators pounced on the objectionable features against which the opposition fought in the commons and unearthed further details of the bureaucrats' grasp for power. They, too, found alarming the government proposal granting the board authority to remake the laws of parliament to suit its own purposes; to discriminate in favour of groups or individuals at the expense of others; declare a resident of Canada, as defined by statute, a non-resident, or vice versa; "make a man a woman", as a member of the house put it. Senator McGeer discovered that disregard for the rights of the individual does not end there. The board could strip its new "creature" naked.
This had to do with the provision requiring that "no person shall, except in accordance with a permit, export any property from Canada." Senator McGeer commented:
This is what I was going to quote:
"You cannot move your own valise out of this country without a permit. They have the power to prevent anyone leaving . . . unless they walk out naked." Coupled with this is the power given the board's agents to search persons suspected of violating the Foreign Exchange Control Act. The Customs Act contains restrictive safeguards so that the traveler, whether he be entering or leaving the country, is left with some dignity. Such consideration of the human being is totally disregarded in the bill before the Senate.
Likewise, as Senator McGeer pointed out, the tourist who wants to come into the country "with his clothes on" must first write to the board for permission. Importation of any property without a permit is banned. Nor is there any recourse to the courts for the individual who might suffer from this abuse of arbitrary authority. No matter what the indignity inflicted, the board's agent has only to plead that he was acting on its instructions, either written or verbal.
Most significant about the Senate's attack was its leadership. It was led by men who were brought up in the same school of political philosophy as those government benchers who bowed their servile heads to the .will of the cabinet. Even Senator Hayden, who was assigned the task of piloting the bill through the upper chamber, proved to be an unenthusiastic sponsor. He confessed that, to his way of thinking, the bill was "unusual" and in some respects "extraordinary."
Senator Lambert doubted whether it would aid in the development of Canada or improve relations with the United States. Senator Bench didn't like it and proposed that life of the legislation be at least limited, the minimum for which the commons opposition fought. Senator Campbell thought that the board should continue to operate for the time being under order in council, where it would be at least subjected to some control by parliament. Senator McGeer, most forthright of all. would have killed it outright.

With this display of acute sensibilities, it is obvious that the bill has few friends in the Senate. It is not what might be regarded as liberal legislation in the proper sense of the word. This being the case, the senators have no choice but drastically to restrict the authority of the board or tell it to carry on under order in council. The Senate cannot possibly sanction the handing over to a group of individuals not responsible to the people "the control over the whole trade and commerce of the nation." As Senator Hayden reminded his colleagues, if the senators approve the bill without putting a limitation on it, they will have parted with their right to deal with it again.
I quoted that editorial because yesterday the Minister of Finance quoted an editorial from the Globe and Mail with such evidence of confidence in the wisdom of their judgment in discussing this matter.

Now, because I find that the Minister of Finance does believe that editorial comment is useful in interpreting his bill, and also because of certain restrictions on the use of the Senate Hansard, I shall quote another editorial which appeared in the Ottawa Journal on August 21, 1946. The heading is, "A disturbed Liberal." I read this editorial because it also dealt with this subject and because the Senate recognized that certain features of this bill were entirely contrary to every principle of Liberalism. The editorial reads:
Senator T. A. Crerar is receiving no end of praise for a speech which he delivered in the Senate last week. Oddly enough, it was a speech in defence of liberalism-against Liberals. Senator Crerar was dealing with a completely totalitarian measure which a Liberal majority in the Commons had sent over to the Senate.
The bill which disturbed Senator Crerar, which made him long for the old liberalism, was one conferring wide powers upon the foreign exchange control board. Said he:
I am still quoting from the editorial.
"This is one of the most extraordinary bills ever to come before the house of parliament. In principle it proposes to confer upon a board of civil servants absolute power over the import and export trade of the country and over the movement of funds across our borders, a power unlimited as to time, and unrestricted as to scope and sweep of operations."
Senator Crerar went on to show, as we in these columns tried to show recently, the extraordinary changes that have come in the political philosophy of this country, with their whittling away all our old ideas of a free economy. Thus:-

I quote again from Senator Crerar:
"I first became a member of parliament thirty years ago and the functions of the government of that day as contrasted with those of the administration of today represent a complete transformation. The government of Canada today is in the wheat business up past its ears. The government is in the housing business to a most extensive degree. It is in the transportation business, by land, sea and air. It is operating a transcontinental air service, ships on the sea and the national railways. The government is in the broadcasting business. The government is in the motion picture business. It is also operating crown companies. It is in the business of dispensing public information. All these activities have completely or at any rate largely changed the functions of government."
That is the end of that quotation from Senator Crerar. It does not say whether or not it was from Hansard.
The picture is not distorted; to an amazing degree Canada has passed from a country of free capitalist effort into one where totalitarianism is steadily on the march. The strange thing, and the pity, is that this transformation has come and continues to come without public discussion, largely without public awareness. The stranger thing, and the greater pity, is that it has been brought about by people who profess to be against totalitarianism, who talk sometimes as if they held the title deeds of liberalism, and. also that many who profess to be the enemies of totalitarianism daily cry out for more of it. We have people, at this moment, calling upon the government to settle strikes by "making the unions work". It does not occur to them that if any government in this -country ever uses force to make the unions work it will not be to make them work for private industry but for the government- the state: that work compelled by force will put us precisely where Russia is and where Germany was.
That is the trouble with too many of us: we have no clear understanding of where all this government intervention, and all this government planning, and all this totalitarian legislation, are carrying us. Well might more of us, whether we belong to labour or to capital, heed the wise words of Senator Crerar.
Again I quote his words, and not from Hansard.

Many members have been urging that the other place initiate more legislation than it
[The Chairman.]
has in earlier years. Certain legislation is initiated in the other place, after which it comes to this house. This practice is in accordance with established practice in Westminster, and, although the procedure in Canada and the United States are not the same, it is an extremely common practice in Washington. So far as one could discern a clear argument yesterday by the Minister of Finance in the speech which he read to the house, it was to the effect that far from our dollar having a normal level below par, it has a level which justifies the fixing of it at 100 cents on the dollar. If it really is so, then these crutches which are now being given the dollar are unnecessary; but the fact is, and the Minister of Finance is well aware of it, that because of perfectly normal and traditional results from the kind of trade that is carried on at the present time between Canada and the United States, our dollar is not at parity with that of the United States.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speechtext:
Because for the whole period covered by the history of international exchange, the value of the money unit of one country in relation to the money unit of another country moves up and down in relation to the balance of trade and other credit considerations between the two countries. And because the convertibility factor was removed from the Bretton Woods agreement we are in the position of dealing alone with the United States, and our excessive purchases in the United States as compared with our exports, naturally, as
Foreign Exchange Control the Minister of Finance well knows, produce a result that does for the time being place our dollar below 100 cents in United States funds.
Probably the unfortunate fact is that our dollar is called a dollar. If it were not called a dollar, then we would not be so sensitive about the normal movement of our unit of exchange. The movement of the unit of exchange is the thing that has controlled and actually brought to a balance the trade between countries, and that is a sound way for our dollar to get back to some measure of parity.
This country need not be so much concerned about the value of its money unit so long as appropriate efforts are made by this government to bring about normal international trading. It is not enough for the Minister of Finance or for any member of this government to say that this is the Bretton Woods agreement; the pound is no longer convertible, and we have just got to go along as we have done in the past. This is a sovereign state. This is a nation which boasts of its great growth and strength in the international sphere. It is the duty of the government of Canada to take steps which will be in keeping with the ultimate needs of this country as one of the greatest trading nations in the world-and it is not only that, but it is one of the greatest per capita trading nations in the world, if not the greatest. Consequently if there is one country which should initiate steps to change this situation and to break the log-jam which has stopped trading in many directions, it is this country, the future of which is so seriously threatened by its inability to sell in markets which would normally be ours.
The Minister of Finance yesterday in the speech which he read-and which obviously he had read over before he presented it here -referred to a statement which I had made on behalf of the province of Ontario in regard to a provision under which the external obligations of provincial governments would be met in such a way as to make it possible for those provinces to pay their obligations at parity in the United States. Not one word of what I put forward, or in what was put forward by anyone else, had to do with this subject of the level of foreign exchange, either then or at any other time. The quotation of the minister yesterday is one of those typical introductions of something which in some way indirectly relates to the subject, and the putting of a coloration upon it to suit his own purpose. He did put a coloration upon it which was improper and which was entirely contrary to the facts, as he well knows.

speechtext:
With the permission of hon. members I might put on record the information I received from the clerk of the house as to the procedure followed in the organization of the standing committees. It is as follows: As soon as standing committees have been set up it is the duty of the chief of the committee branch of the house to call a meeting of each of them for the purpose of electing its chairman. In doing so he endeavours to suit the conveniences of the members of the house and he consults the chief government whip as to the day on which they will be free to attend.
As some members belong to two or three committees, it is the usual practice to have all of the committees choose their chairmen on the same day. A few days elapse before this first meeting because some consultation has to take place prior to the choice of the chairmen.

Alter committees have been fully organized by the appointment of their chairmen, they enjoy complete autonomy within the orders of reference sent to them by the house. They are free to settle the dates of their meetings and to regulate their own proceedings. Interference of members or even ministers of the crown with their proceedings would be considered a breach of privilege.
They are responsible to the house alone, and in no way subservient to the government.
Arthur Beauchesne,
Clerk of the House of Commons

speechtext:
In the province of British Columbia we are faced with the problem of having to sell a great deal of our lumber, our canned salmon, our apples, our base metals and other commodities to Great Britain and other commonwealth countries. As everyone knows there is great difficulty at present in connection with that trade. The apple trade, and I think also the trade in canned salmon, have been cut off completely, though there is still some lumber going to Britain.
From time to time the suggestion has been advanced that an arrangement could be made under which we would bring in steel from Great Britain in exchange for our lumber, for example. I realize that there are obstacles to the setting up of this kind of trade, but in reading the report of the foreign exchange control board I gathered the idea that the board is not very keen about arrangements
Foreign Exchange Control of the kind. At page 7, for example, we And reference to two types of arrangements which could be made to promote trade between dollar and non-dollar countries. The first suggestion is that the exporting country, which in my case would be Canada, should advance credits to the importing country, in my case Great Britain. The other suggestion is that arrangements be made for special deals in which the exporting country, which would be Canada, agreed to use the proceeds of its exports to take more goods from its dollar-short customer even though those goods were higher in price than if bought elsewhere. That would mean bringing steel from Great Britain for use in British Columbia.
I would like the Minister of Finance to explain the attitude of the board and of the government toward transactions of that kind, because it does seem to me we are in a corner as far as this trade is concerned. We are like the dog that had to climb a tree; we have to do something. I should like to know why it is not possible for Canada to work out some special arrangement under which we could exchange British Columbia timber, for example, for steel from Great Britain.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, of course that involves a very large question of trade policy. Arrangements of that kind, if carried on to any great extent, essentially would involve what are commonly known as barter deals; that is to say, one country arranges to swap a certain quantity of wheat, let us say, or bacon, for a certain quantity of steel or manufactured goods. That sort of thing involves a substantial degree of import control on the part of both countries. It involves, if it is to be carried through to any substantial extent, a considerable degree of state trading, that is purchases by the state. But perhaps the most difficult feature of an arrangement of that kind is that the price of the steel, as my hon. friend has indicated, may be higher than the price at which that steel could be obtained from our domestic producers, let us say, or from producers in the United States. Someone would have to pay that higher cost, either the purchaser or the taxpayers as a whole.
Many other difficulties are involved in arrangements of that kind. Incidentally I understand that the board of trade in Great Britain has arranged for a substantial increase in exports of steel to this country, through representations made by my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I do not know the price, but I assume the steel is coming in at reasonably competitive prices.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: Higher prices.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
The demand for steel is such that Canadian consumers are prepared to

Foreign Exchange Control pay those higher prices. But let me say to my hon. friend that we in Canada are not only ready but anxious to take any sort of commodity, capital or consumer goods, that the United Kingdom is able to export to us at competitive prices. We are not only ready; we are extremely anxious to do that, and we have gone to quite considerable lengths, as I shall attempt to indicate in the course of my budget speech in dealing with trade questions, to encourage that type of export, and we hope and believe the steps we have taken and that are being taken by western European countries will result in an increased flow of trade to this country.
In direct answer to my hon. friend's question, I do not believe that a system of barter deals is in the interests of Canada if it can possibly be avoided, if for no other reason than that such a tremendous volume of both our imports and our exports come from and go to the United States. We cannot make barter deals with the United States; they do not operate on that basis. We have to operate on a price basis there, and naturally that introduces very serious complications in the matter of barter deals with other coun-' tries, which in my judgment are most undesirable in the interests of Canada as a whole.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: Surely the minister does not mean these deals necessarily would have to be made between governments. Suppose a lumber-producing firm in British Columbia exchanged lumber for steel, and then disposed of that steel in British Columbia.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: There is nothing to prevent that. It would be splendid.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: That is a private transaction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: But as I read the report of the foreign exchange control board, that board is not favourable to deals of that kind. I am not an expert on this question, but it does seem to me there is a method there of getting our trade with Great Britain back to something approaching normal. It does seem the foreign exchange control board is not working very hard to bring about deals such as the one I have mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
On the contrary, Mr. Speaker,
I do not think there is any objection, let us say, to a British Columbia producer of lumber entering into an arrangement with a British steel manufacturer to swap lumber for steel. The British Columbia producer would then be faced with the problem of selling steel in Canada at competitive prices. He may be unwilling to take that risk and, as to that, I do not know
[Mr. Abbott 1

Generally speaking, the foreign exchange control board would put no obstacle in the way of an arrangement of that type. Far from doing anything to discourage imports from sterling area countries, the foreign exchange control board and every other agency of government is doing everything in its power to encourage such imports. It is tremendously in the interests of the Canadian people as a whole to do that because of the volume of our export trade. We should try to get our customers in a position where they can pay for our goods. It was for that reason we extended these large credits, so these countries would be able to restore their productive machinery and export goods and services to us. This is the only real way in which our exports can be paid for. They cannot be paid for in pieces of paper; they have to be paid for in something tangible. When these importing countries are able to restore their economies to the position which enables them to export goods and services to us and to other countries at prices which our people are willing to pay, then our trading accounts can be balanced.

speechtext: Is there any agency or department of government which is actively promoting such transactions, such as helping the exchange of steel from Great Britain for lumber from Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce

Mr. Chairman, if I may answer that question, the Department of Trade and Commerce encourages barter deals where they are helpful. The barter deal which my friend proposes would not be helpful. He proposes that a producer of lumber in British Columbia exchange that lumber for steel from Great Britain. May I point out that we are taking now all the steel Britain can send us and we are exporting all the lumber Britain will take from us.
The trade is just as badly unbalanced if you take $50 million worth of lumber on one side and $50 million worth of steel on the other side out of our reciprocal trade accounts; your unbalance continues unchanged. True, one individual transaction is balanced, but since you have a large movement of each of the two commodities, the unbalance is continued just as if your barter deal never took place.
Last year our department helped to work out a barter deal with Brazil in which apples were exchanged for oranges. This was a helpful transaction because the oranges would not have moved to Canada otherwise and we would not have had that market for our apples. It is the latter type of barter

deal that we encourage because it develops new trade. The department has attempted to develop other barter deals, but some have not worked out. Such a transaction usually has to be developed at somewhat higher prices than competitive prices in one of the countries concerned. We do everything possible to encourage the type of deal I have mentioned whenever it develops new trade between countries and I may say the foreign exchange control board has put no obstacles in the way of such transactions.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: Is that the type of barter deal that is taking place between Great Britain and the other countries in the sterling area?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: I do not know; it is difficult to say. 1 believe those transactions are not true barter deals. It is really an agreement to buy so much wheat from Russia, we will say, as against so much machinery from England. To the best of my information the settlements have been made partly in pounds sterling or in dollars. In other words, the transactions are not barter deals as I understand that term. These transactions seem to be mutual trade deals in that the settlement is not strictly goods for goods.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: This word "barter" is being used a great deal now and I do not understand exactly what is meant by it. Will the minister explain what he meant by calling this deal with Brazil a barter deal?

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: In the barter deal to which I referred, the people in British Columbia said they would exchange so many boxes of apples for so many boxes of oranges. It was simply an exchange of goods for goods.

speechtext:
The Minister of Finance, I think, will agree that one of the reasons Britain has to charge high prices for some exports is that under the special agreements which she has with European nations she is able to get those high prices. If we want these goods to come to Canada we will have to compete and pay those prices. I should like to refer the minister to a statement I quoted last night appearing in the foreign exchange control board report near the bottom of page 6:
If efforts on the part of the sterling area and ERP countries in the direction of greater exports to dollar countries are inadequate or fail to solve their dollar problem, then it may be expected that these countries will continue to place special restrictions on imports from dollar countries. The countries whose exports are affected by these restrictions will be confronted with the choice of finding some alternative use, at home or in other foreign markets, for the goods previously exported to the dollar-short countries or making special arrangements in an effort to retain these markets. These arrangements could involve the provision of the exports without payment in foreign exchange, through the extension of grants or credits,-
This is the point I wish to emphasize.
-or special deals in which the exporting country agreed to use the proceeds of its exports to take more goods from its dollar-short customers even though these goods were higher in price than had to be paid elsewhere. To make room for these relatively high-priced imports it would be necessary to impose discriminatory import restrictions.
I wonder if the minister could explain just what kind of deals the board had in mind when they said:
-or special deals in which the exporting country agreed to use the proceeds of its exports to take more goods from its dollar-short customers even though these goods were higher in price than had to be paid elsewhere.
This would mean we would be importing goods into this country at higher prices than prevailed within Canada. No doubt that would mean we would have to subsidize those imports. We did not hesitate to subsidize imports into this country during the war in order to maintain the price ceiling. Surely, if it is a question of maintaining our markets in Europe, we would be justified in going to the length of subsidizing imports. If we are not prepared to compete with other nations for British goods because the prices are higher, we must lose that market and we may have a great deal of difficulty in getting it back.
Surely, as a short-time expedient, it might be well worth our while to subsidize imports into this country, thus making it possible for the importer to sell them at existing price

Foreign Exchange Control levels. This foreign exchange control board report says:
To make room for these relatively high-priced imports it would be necessary to impose discriminatory import restrictions.
Would that not come into conflict with the Geneva trade agreements?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: Unquestionably.

In principle, yes. On the other hand there are escape clauses in the Geneva trade agreement which would appear to permit action of that type. I know the minister spoke last year about these escape clauses and the advantage taken of them in trading. They were going to live up to the principle. What is the use of having an escape clause in an agreement if you are not going to utilize it? Surely when we are faced with a situation that is as serious as the situation today, where our markets to Britain are in danger of shrinking, we would be justified in utilizing a clause that was put in there for the very purpose for which we may need it in this case.
In view of the serious situation in regard to our exports to Britain, I should like to ask the minister whether he would not consider the advisability of accepting sterling in payment for our exports; then using the sterling in the purchase of British goods, even if the prices of those British goods were higher than the price level in this country; and then placing a subsidy on the prices of those goods so that importers could sell them at the existing price level in this country. The minister himself will admit that that procedure would not be a violation of the Geneva trade agreements, if it were done under the escape clauses.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
First, the hon. member for Acadia has raised a difficult and serious question, namely, the extent to which this country is going into the business of subsidizing high-cost imports into Canada which are in competition in this market, subsidizing wage levels of this country or that country which are lower or higher than ours.
I cannot agree with the dark picture that he has painted as to the trade prospects in the sterling area market. It is true those countries are going through a difficult period at this time. We knew they would be going through a difficult period. That is why we extended substantial credits. That is why the United States government is extending these substantial credits under ERP. It may well be that, when the period of the European recovery plan expires, the western European countries will not have achieved the degree of self-sufficiency or restoration of their economy they now anticipate.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: That is evident.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: Although we must recognize- and I have said so on a number of occasions -that we must look forward to some diminution of our exports to those particular countries, I do not take the dark view that others appear to take when they say they will be drastically curtailed. So far as our main primary products are concerned, I believe they will be maintained. But I think we must face the fact that in a number of fields, and particularly in the field of manufactured goods, we must look to greater access to other markets, particularly the United States market. But let me say this. Until the situation becomes much worse than it is now, or much worse than I expect it will be, I would be strongly opposed to any system of subsidizing high-cost imports.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: I would point out that the cost of that procedure might be much less than the cost to this country of losing markets for our primary products.

speechtext: Let us settle that question, but let us not settle it on a hypothetical basis. A moment ago I made the statement that we have not lost these markets. We have not lost them by any means. subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951

speechtext:
I tried to make clear yesterday that I attached great importance as well, notwithstanding its comparative ineffectiveness up until now, to the international monetary fund and to its operation. I tried to emphasize the fact that I regretted certain aspects of its administration and operation up until now. I want to ask the Minister of Finance certain questions with regard to our relationship to that fund. I want to know just how we keep in touch with it. I understand we have a representative there. I want to ask just what our method of contact is, or how closely we keep in touch. Then I should like to ask the minister to indicate to us whether we are consulted with regard to the various things that arise, and how we deal
Foreign Exchange Control with the questions that arise. In particular I should like to ask him to indicate whether there is any indication that the various governments which are members of the agreement are prepared for forward action. Rumours come out from time to time-and I stress the fact that they are rumours- that the officials themselves at the headquarters of the fund are anxious for more flexibility and are anxious to move forward but that as yet they have not been supported by the people back home. As I say, it is rumour; I do not put it forward as anything more than that.
I want to read one sentence from the report of the international monetary fund. It is found on page 1 of the report of 1948 and is as follows:
The restoration of international balance, however, still requires important and difficult adjustments in many national economies and for most of these adjustments the national authorities now have the main responsibility.
I take it that in a broad way that means that the officials of the fund are indicating in this statement that I have read, that they are only instruments, or agents, and that the principals are the various countries. I have indicated a rather broad range of questions, but I wish the minister would tell us, in what detail he can, just what our means of contact is, just what relationship we have to the fund, and just what reason there is, if any, to suggest that the fund is trying to think its way forward, or whether it is going to remain static. In the latter case it seems to me that the prospects of its doing the tremendous task which it was set up to do are not at all bright.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: I do not know just how much territory my hon. friend expects me to cover.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
I
should like the minister to cover a wide area.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
I will do the best I can. As the hon. member is probably aware, the international monetary fund is set up under the terms of the Bretton Woods Agreements Act, which was adopted by this house in 1945. The organization of the fund consists of governors who are the finance ministers for the time being of the respective countries which are members of the fund. For the time being I am the governor of the fund representing Canada, and as such I have attended the annual meetings of the fund, which take place once a year. In 1947 the annual meeting took place in London. In 1948, in September, it took place in Washington. The executive of the fund consists of a body known as the executive directors, and these executive directors are selected by vote of members of

Foreign Exchange Control the fund. The system of votes is rather complicated. I have not got it in my head, and I shall not attempt to explain it here, but broadly speaking the bigger countries, the United Kingdom, France, the United States, China-I am not sure whether it includes anybody else-have enough votes of their own to elect an executive director of the fund. Other countries must combine to select an executive director. At the present time Canada has an executive director on the fund in the person of Mr. Rasminsky of the Bank of Canada who, as my hon. friend knows, is the alternative chairman of the foreign exchange control board. Mr. Rasminsky attends the meetings of the executive directors of the fund in Washington at pretty regular intervals. It partly depends upon the business which is before the fund. He does not go there for all the meetings, but the constitution of the fund provides for alternate directors.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
Do we
have a representative there permanently?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
I am coming to that. Each of the executive directors has what is known as an alternate, and Canada's alternate is Mr. J. F. Parkinson, who is the financial attache at our embassy in Washington. At meetings at which it is not possible for Mr. Rasminsky to be present, Mr. Parkinson attends. He has constant contact with the executive of the fund itself. As my hon. friend is aware, the chairman is Mr. Camille Gutt, a former minister of finance of Belgium. He is the executive head of the fund. In addition to the executive directors, the fund has quite a large, and in my judgment quite a competent, executive staff; that is to say, a staff of experts on currency matters and monetary matters, research people and the like. I understand that they are constantly studying these international currency and exchange problems. When specific questions come up, which the fund agreement requires to be dealt with by the fund, they are submitted by the countries concerned. An instance is the action which Canada took a little over a year ago last November to introduce our system of assistance to the gold mining industry. The original plan which we had was considered by the fund as a possible infringement of the fund agreement. I do not know that we were in complete accord with that view, but at any rate the proposals were modified, submitted to the fund, and approved.
The fund will sometimes take action on its own initiative. My hon. friend will recall that it did so recently in the case of the sale by South Africa of 100,000 ounces of gold, ostensibly for commercial purposes, at a price 
some $6.50 above the $35 United States, which is the price established by the United States treasury.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: What was the action?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: I have not the data here. It first made an inquiry of the government of South Africa, expressing grave doubts as to the desirability, and perhaps even the propriety, of the arrangement under the fund agreement, and after receiving certain explanations from the government of South Africa, issued a further statement in which it again indicated that it felt there were serious grounds for believing that this gold would not go into the regular commercial or industrial channels, but would be going into channels which were prohibited under the fund.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: Who was the purchaser of the gold?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: I have forgotten the name; I believe it was some firm of gold brokers in London.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: Johannesburg?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: They may have had an office in Johannesburg, but they have connections elsewhere. Generally, I think this is the way in which the fund operates. I cannot pretend to be an expert on these international monetary fund matters. When questions come before the fund which involve matters of policy, Canada's executive director on the fund consults me, and if it is a matter which requires cabinet consideration I report to my colleagues; but generally speaking that is the way in which the fund operates.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
Can
the minister say whether in fact there has been any consideration by the executive officers of the fund with their governmental principals as to the modifications in the original arrangement with a view to what I, at any rate, would regard as desirable elasticity, or were they just content to ride along as is?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: So far as I am aware, the executive directors of the fund do not consider that the provisions of the fund agreement, with the latitude which these provisions allow for change of exchange rates, are as yet inadequate, and with that view I am in agreement.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
Just one final question. Am I correct in assuming that, so far as the minister is aware, the present situation which has led us into something near an impasse with regard to our relation with the sterling area is apparently

contemplated with equanimity by the directors of the fund and the various governments, and that there is no move on foot to try to meet the situation which the Minister of Agriculture so eloquently described in accurate terms. I want to know whether that is true. In other words, if this fund, which was set up with such high hope three years ago, has really stalled and, if I understand the minister correctly, no consideration is being given to the introduction of any further element of elasticity in a situation with the dangers and difficulties which not only the Minister of Agriculture but the Minister of Finance himself will admit, then the situation is indeed a serious one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
The difficulties which the United Kingdom or other western European countries may be involved in, in connection with their trade, are not due to any exchange difficulties created by the international monetary fund. The international monetary fund has no power to impose upon any of its members a particular exchange rate. It has the right to approve changes; it has the right to make recommendations; but it has no power to impose upon any one of its members any particular exchange rate.
As I say, the difficulties of the United Kingdom and others in exporting their goods are not due to exchange difficulties as such. They are due to the fact that these areas are not as yet producing enough goods and services to pay for what they have to buy from this particular area of the world. That is the fundamental underlying cause. It may be-I am not suggesting that it is-that some of these European currencies are overvalued. It is not for me to say whether they are or not. If they are overvalued, then it is perfectly clear that that is a bar to their export trade; but that is not something which Canada can solve for itself, and it is certainly not something that the international monetary fund can solve.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
First of all the minister said that currency had nothing to do with these trade difficulties. Later on he said much more correctly that if in fact currencies were overvalued they did have something to do with it. In the last statement he was right. But when he says that Canada cannot do anything about it, may I say this. We have talked pretty big about ourselves. The government have talked pretty big about the wonderful things they have done, which I prefer to say that we have done, and we have done pretty well. We are not going to take the position that we are a nonentity and that it is not possible for us to have thoughts of our own, and that if we have those thoughts they would not be listened to
Foreign Exchange Control if they were presented to the fund. Whether I am right or not is not the point. I should like to know whether the minister is taking the position that there is nothing that Canada can do; in other words, that if Canada had views that she wished to have carried out there is nothing we can do to have them accepted by the fund. If that is right, then I think we should seriously consider withdrawing from the fund. But I do not think it is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: I know that my hon. friend wants to be constructive. I am going to ask him a question after I make a statement. As a nation, Canada has no right to change the exchange rate of any other nation; and believe me, we would resent it pretty strongly if any other nation attempted to tell us what we should do in that regard. As Minister of Finance I would consider such advice from any other country as purely gratuitous and impertinent. I would not presume to offer any advice to any other country as to what exchange rate it should place on its currency. My question to my hon. friend is this-

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: Isn't the result that we cannot buy from them?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: Now, this is a technical subject, and I should be pleased if the hon. member would allow me to complete my thoughts. I said to my hon. friend from Muskoka-Ontario that the international monetary fund has no right to impose an exchange rate on any other country. It has the right to endeavour to persuade, but it has not the right to impose its will-and rightly so-because I do not think that any body of that kind should supersede the sovereignty of any particular nation. Now, my question to the hon. member is this, and I know he wants to be constructive. I would ask him what positive measure he suggests Canada should take in the situation he has outlined?

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
One of
the greatest advantages held out-and correctly so-in the international monetary fund was that it provided a forum where people could sit around a table and discuss their difficulties. That was one of the great points made-and rightly so-when we had evidence before the committee on banking and commerce three years ago. What I am suggesting is that at the very least we can get that body together. Secondly-and I am not going into details nor am I going to repeat what I said yesterday-I suggest for what it is worth that what we are considering now is whether we are condemned to what I still call a kind of paralysing inaction. Because how we can sit here contemplating the shrinkage of our markets is beyond me.

Foreign Exchange Control I am not so optimistic as the minister permits himself to be with regard to the situation in western Europe, if this situation continues. The minister made a statement about not wanting advice from other countries as to how we should value our dollar. Now, if the minister will not take advice from us I am sure he will not take it from anybody.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: There are others I would sooner take advice from.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
But I
am coming back to this-and this is my point. The Minister of Finance keeps on saying that we are not going to do anything about this, that there is no suggestion we are going to make. I suggest to him that monetary things are not going well; they are going badly. And I say again, page the Minister of Agriculture. Because while the Minister of Agriculture was not able, and while no one is able, in an offhand way, to suggest how it is going to be done, in the meantime the minister sits here, stares in the face of something which is of immense importance to the western plains, and says there is nothing he can do about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: No, I am not saying there is nothing I can do about it. But I am saying that we cannot cure it by currency manipulation, either of the Canadian currency or of some other.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
I am
not suggesting currency manipulation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: What are you suggesting?

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
In one
of his more accurate moments, the minister said a moment ago that, if there was any overvaluation of the exchange, that was what would injure trade. There is a widespread feeling-and I pointed this out yesterday in my remarks-that some of the European exchanges are overvalued. Read the report of the governor of the Bank of Canada. It says that you now have the sterling area up in a kind of ivory tower. What will the effect be? The effect of it will be that trade with the sterling area will become more and more difficult and you are not doing anything about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
I am
not asking the minister to say it. All I say is that we are deeply interested in it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951

And
one of the points of the monetary fund was to get the various parties interested to come together to consider if anything that may be done has not been done.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951

It would appear, to an
unobservant person, that we were not making any progress. But when we find the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario and the Minister of Finance both agreeing that they do not know what to do about this situation, I think that is an indication that we are moving. The reason they do not know what to do about it is that they are not operating in old familiar grooves or old patterns. Trade patterns are not what they were twenty-five or thirty years ago, or perhaps even less than that. A new situation has developed. Two world wars have perhaps permanently affected our economy.
What we have to do is to try and reconstruct trade and business on a basis that fits in with the present-day conditions. The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario looks with longing eyes on what was, and the Minister of Finance, who is orthodox in the extreme, is also looking back to things as they once were, and as he would like them again to be.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
No, we
are Progressive Conservatives.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
