subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951

speechtext:
It is an interesting fact that when the charter for Bretton Woods was prepared it specifically mentioned that those joining would be admitted with their currency at the rate of exchange it enjoyed at the time of their admission. When that discussion was going on in this house our dollar was at 90 cents as compared with the United States dollar. They made the further proviso that the currency of a country could not be depreciated more than 10 per cent without the consent of the fund.
My point is that they recognized the trading advantage of a depreciated currency; otherwise they never would have put in that proviso and placed a limit on the extent to which your currency could be depressed. Having regard to the fact that the traders of the world and men versed in finance paid great attention to that provision, it did seem to me most unusual that Canada should move out of the preferred position she enjoyed at that time, by placing our dollar at par when we were in a position to join Bretton Woods with a 90-cent dollar which could have fluctuated from that pivot point either backward or forward, within the regulations laid down by the fund.
Having recited these facts, since these various trading agencies were brought into being to promote multilateral trade though practically all we have today is bilateral trade, I want to ask the minister whether it was not intended that you could trade in a circle, and that this international monetary fund would adjust your trading balance so we would avoid the very thing we have been hearing about, that is barter trade. In other words, we completed our deal with Brazil, and Brazil completed a deal with somebody else. Eventually through this bank, in which we made a substantial deposit in gold or in kind which was recognized as acceptable, our balance should be adjusted there, and we should have been able to use our trading organizations, the industry of our people, and business and commerce generally in order to go out and seek markets throughout the world. As long as the United States dollar remained the standard of value, it would take a great deal to convince me that we did not enjoy a trading advantage over the United States in connection with the

Foreign Exchange Control goods we were capable of producing in great quantities, because our productive capacity was so large in relation to the demand of the home market. We could have had these advantages in the world market if we had taken full advantage of the trading organizations that have been set up.
So I ask what progress if any has been made along the line of making it possible to engage in multilateral trade or even trading within a circle, in which we could expect to have our currency exchanged for the currency we use at the international bank.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
Well, as I indicated in my remarks yesterday, the change in value of the Canadian dollar in July, 1946, was made because of inflationary forces at work in the United States at that time, and to prevent a further price rise in Canada. In my judgment, as I said yesterday, Canada could have derived no trading advantage by continuing its dollar at a ten per cent discount in relation to the United States dollar. During the last three years we have sold every bit of the produce of this country we had to sell, in quantities greater than we ever sold before, and at competitive prices. So, as I demonstrated yesterday, I do not think anyone can accurately assert that the Canadian dollar is overvalued and that we need to depreciate it in terms of United States currency. Our problem has been that our customers have not been able to get the wherewithal to pay us.
On my hon. friend's second question, as to what progress has been made with respect to restoring multilateral trade, I can only answer him by saying that I am afraid there has been lamentably little progress. It was recognized, of course, when the international monetary fund was first considered and when it was brought into existence, that during the period immediately following the war, which was referred to as the transition period, for which special provision was made, it could play only a perhaps relatively minor role in helping to even out these currency distortions. It was never contemplated that it could correct an unbalance arising out of substantial capital expenditures, for instance. That is what has been taking place in western European countries in recent years. A great deal of the imports which those countries have had to make from Canada and the United States have been to restore their factories, their houses, their machinery and other things which were destroyed as a result of the war. It was never contemplated that an organization such as the international monetary fund could possibly do more than help to even out the temporary unbalances in current account transactions. It can never, consequently, ful-


fil its full role until western Europe and these other countries have been restored to their full productive capacity.

I want to make this observation. The minister said we have sold everything we have for export. Let us consider how this was accomplished.
First of all, we lent a great deal of the money with which to purchase these goods and we relied largely upon ERP to take up the balance. It was quite evident from the minister's remarks on the radio in November of last year that we did lack United States currency. There is no question about that. It was also very evident that we were storing up a large volume of United States currency when we had the ninety-cent dollar. Many United States tourists came to this country, and for my part, their trade is very valuable. Up in Georgian bay we spend a great deal of money to attract these people to that part of the country. If those people could come here and get a dollar and ten cents' worth of goods for their dollar, it was worth encouraging them because the goods were produced here.
Conversely, we have restrictions upon our own people traveling to the United States. With the ninety-cent dollar, if our people wanted to sacrifice a dollar and ten cents to go to the United States and wanted to pay a dollar and ten cents for goods worth a dollar, that was up to them. This ninety-cent dollar, however, tended to restrict those imports which have played havoc with our internal economy. In the final analysis the funds upon which we depend to provide us with the means whereby we can trade multilaterally have failed. The government has been lax in its efforts in promoting the better interests of the trade of Canada. The government has leaned upon ERP and when ERP is finished- well, probably this government will be finished before then and there will be an opportunity for us to do something on our own behalf. The government has become a leaner on the United States and has tied our dollar to the United States dollar, failing to see that our great advantages are in the sterling area.

There are some figures appearing in a return from the Department of Trade and Commerce which I should like to quote to the Minister of Finance in respect to the United Kingdom. The United Kingdom's imports from Canada in 1948 amounted to $688 million, whereas Canada's imports from the United Kingdom amounted to only $274 million. When we come to South Africa we find they exported to Canada $3,522,000 worth of goods, whereas Canada sold to South Africa $83 million worth of goods. Turning to another sterling area country, Jamaica, they purchased from Canada, in 1948, $12,371,000 worth of goods, whereas we purchased from that country only $9 million worth of goods. Trinidad and Tobago purchased from Canada $17 million worth of goods, whereas we purchased from them only $8,990,000 worth of goods. Australia imported from Canada $38 million worth of goods, whereas in 1948 we purchased from Australia only $22 million. New Zealand purchased from Canada $18 million in goods whereas we purchased from that country only $11 million in goods.
My suggestion to the minister is this. Is it not a fact that the Canadian dollar is depreciated to such an extent in the eyes of the sterling area countries that they are not willing to sell to us?

We are extremely anxious to import from these various countries as much 29087-103i
Foreign Exchange Control as we can. We have done all kinds of things to encourage those imports, and I shall have occasion to say a good deal about that later on a more appropriate occasion. World trading accounts between two different countries have never exactly balanced, and that goes back, I was going to say, to the prehistoric days mentioned by the hon. member for Mus-koka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) when he spoke of barter. The whole system of world trading presupposes that you use your surplus from one area to offset your balance in another area. That has been the traditional pattern of Canadian trade. We have always purchased twice as much from the United States as we sold to that country. We have been using our surplus accumulated from other areas to restore the balance. We have been going to great lengths to encourage imports from those countries to which my hon. friend has referred. It is very much in our interest to do so.
May I say that the imports must be things which our people are willing to use, and they must be at a price which is somewhere near what our people are prepared to pay. That is the fundamental reason why we are not importing more. I suppose we could buy a lot of New Zealand butter.
I do not know how the population would react to that, but we might do it. We used to sell a great many motor cars to New Zealand, but I do not know whether or not we do today. Perhaps the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) would know. In any event, the failure of those countries to export to Canada, let me assert again, is not the fault of Canada.

The Minister of Finance has just emphasized the government's determination to encourage imports from the sterling countries. I would suggest to him one very good way he could encourage at least some imports from the sterling countries would be to take the sterling area out of the provisions of schedule I of the Emergency Exchange Conservation Act.
Under that act, which was passed last year, a total prohibition was placed on the importation of certain goods from all countries, including the sterling area. We all knew, and the government knew, that the real problem to be met then was that our purchases in the United States were too high. It was United States imports that should have been prohibited; but the government prohibited imports from all countries, including the sterling area. Surely the time has now come when the sterling area can be lifted out of schedule I of the Emergency Exchange Conservation Act. I notice in the annual report

Foreign Exchange Control of the operations under that act, for the calendar year 1948, that there were a good many million dollars involved in these goods which were prohibited from the non-schedule countries, which in effect means from the sterling area. I would ask the minister why he cannot remove the sterling area now from the provisions of that schedule I.

That is the fact. I asserted that fact in this house when those measures were under consideration, and the event has proved that I was right; because the imports from the sterling area countries, in spite of higher : prices-particularly in textiles-have substantially increased and imports of course from hard-currency countries have substantially decreased.

The minister need not be nervous. He has sitting beside him another capable minister in the person of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who will listen to the remarks I intend to make. Between the two of them perhaps they may work out some plan whereby what I say may make the lot of both ministers easier and in addition may make things much better for Canada. Last year, in 1948, I believe we imported from the United States approximately five million tons of hard coal. It was a little bit more than that, but I will use round figures. For that coal we paid $54 million. That sum had to be paid in good United States currency. If there was any premium on their dollar, we of course had to pay that extra. To bring that coal from the United States mines to our border cost us approximately $13 million. I know that we must deal with the United States; I shall not try to put up an argument as to whether we should not buy coal from them. But I argue that a great deal of that coal should be purchased here in Canada. Recently in the Albertan, published in Calgary-it is an excellent paper; it is always right up to date-there was an editorial, in which was quoted an exchange between the Minister of Trade and Commerce and myself a short time ago when I asked a question as to whether it would be possible for the minis-
Foreign Exchange Control ter to assure hard coal users in Ontario that a spur line could be built in from Okotoks, Alberta, to the hard-coal mine on the Sheep river fifty miles west of Okotoks. The editorial makes a significant statement. It is all significant but I shall quote only one statement, which is as follows:
Still very much in question, however, is the economic problem of getting a railway constructed to the mine, and the political question of what effect the large-scale operation of this coal property would have on existing coal operations.
Previously I had given no thought to the political effect. I am not interested in what the political effect is on any party in Canada, not even this party. I am interested in creating trade in Canada. I spent much of my life trying to create trade in Canada, internal trade as well as foreign trade. I should like to see the Minister of Trade and Commerce help the Minister of Finance to ease his problem of foreign exchange by taking some action whereby people in Ontario, who use so much hard coal, five million tons a year, could buy at least half of it in Canada.
On my desk I have a lump of Alberta hard coal which came down from the mine I went to see last fall. It is as fine a piece of hard coal as I have ever seen in my lifetime from any mine anywhere, and compares with anything that can be produced in Pennsylvania. I know something about coal. You cannot beat this coal anywhere. I am trying to be constructive.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: May I see it?

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: How does it compare with Welsh anthracite?

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: That is why I asked to see it.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
Welsh anthracite is another grade altogether. There is Pennsylvania anthracite and then there is Welsh anthracite. They are both called anthracite, but they are not of the same texture. This is Alberta anthracite, which is a different texture again. It is a high grade hard coal. I am not personally interested in coal in any shape, manner or form. As a Canadian I am interested only in doing two or three things: firstly, providing employment for Canadians to mine the coal; secondly, providing freight for our railways; and thirdly, cutting down exchange.
The minister has a difficult problem on his hands, and it is up to us to ease the burden if we can. In using Alberta hard coal we could save millions of dollars in exchange which the minister has to find to bring in United States hard coal. I am not an authority on coal, but I have discussed this with the very best engineers who are themselves

Foreign Exchange Control authorities on the properties of this coal. I have read the report of the coal board, but I have not much faith in it, I am sorry to say. I am not going to condemn it, but it does not seem to me to be a report designed to encourage the development of coal in Canada. That is what I want to do. I want to encourage the development of coal in Canada. The report is tinged with arguments against this hard coal, and I do not know whether any of the people who wrote the report were ever there. I was there. I did not go at government expense. I went to the mine that this lump of coal came from. If I remember rightly, this lump of coal came from 1,400 feet in the tunnel. It was just knocked off the wall and came down to me here.
I want to make my argument as short as I can. If we can mine hard coal in Canada- I know of nowhere else in Canada where we can mine hard coal-it would look to me that every effort should be made by Canadians to do it and thus ease the burden of the Minister of Finance.
Last year we purchased five million tons of hard coal in the United States. We should try within five or ten years' time to produce two and a half million tons of hard coal in Canada. That would be a target to aim at. At the rate we paid for the coal last year, that would mean a saving of $27 million in United States money. Added to that would *be approximately $13 million in United States freight. I am aware that we have a problem, Mr. Chairman. The cars which would come down here full of coal would have to go back to Alberta empty; but we have to do that with our wheat cars, our cattle cars and everything else. In any event it would be our own money; it would not be outside money that we would have to pay to send the cars back empty. I believe we can put our teeth into this problem. If we expanded the soft coal market, too, we would save much more. We buy twenty-five million tons of soft coal a year from outside of Canada. For both hard coal and soft coal we sent out of Canada last year $181 million. That was United States dollars that the minister had to buy, and to bring the coal into Canada the minister had to find approximately $70 million of United States exchange for freight. Therefore for every ton of coal, either hard or soft, that we produce in Canada, we would be saving exchange money. I am speaking particularly of hard coal because in Toronto we want to use Alberta hard coal.
I am not interested in this company in any shape, manner or form; I cannot give the right name of it. The mine I am thinking of is called the Burns mine in Alberta. I wish the hon. member for Calgary West were


here. If he were he could handle this much better than I can. He made a magnificent speech last night and I had hoped that he would deal with this question too. I had intended to get him up on his feet today to speak on it; but since he is not in at the moment I shall try to do the best I can. Since I am an Ontario man my heart is in the effort to try to use Alberta hard coal. I think the company is called the Alberta Hard Coal Company. They brought down about fifteen cars of coal during the last few months. It has been thoroughly tested in a hundred homes in Toronto. I went to see it in operation. The users of it are loud in their praise of its quality. It is good hard coal. It burns to an ash and throws off much heat. I asked the users how it compared with Pennsylvania hard coal, and they gave the edge to the Alberta hard coal. I would ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce to use his best endeavours to try to have a spur line put in to that coal mine. What does it mean? At the moment they are selling this coal in Toronto, good hard coal, at $17 a ton. That means that the users in Toronto have $3.75 left in their pocket for every ton of coal used. The producers of the coal have to pay $4 a ton to have it trucked from the mine to Okotoks or wherever they load it on to the railways. I do not think it is Okotoks; it is another station ten miles nearer Calgary, at a place called Midnapore. The trucking to Midnapore costs them $4 a ton. If we had a spur line in there it would mean $4 less a ton to the Toronto coal users, which would mean that the price would be approximately $14 or less a ton.
I have participated in this debate to try to throw out some suggestions whereby the burdens of the Minister of Finance could be eased. There are two billion tons of hard coal we can have from Alberta, which would make the minister's burden much lighter. I would have to persuade the Minister of Transport to use his best endeavours with the railway company to put that spur in. It would be paid for in one year's time through the savings in amounts paid for coal by Canadian coal users, and it would take off the shoulders of the Minister of Finance a portion of the heavy burden he now carries in providing United States dollars for United States coal.
I thank you, Mr. Chairman, and hon. members for the patience you have shown in listening to me. I have made my suggestions honestly and earnestly, after much travel and endeavour; and I am going to keep it up until Canadians are enabled to use Canadian hard coal, thus saving themselves $4 or $5 on every ton they use.

speechtext: Earlier in the afternoon the minister intimated that he was not concerned with the loss of British markets. I rather gathered from him that the British markets were not being lost. speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
I have been listening on a number of occasions, not only during this debate but during one or two others, to the references that have been made to Great Britain. I want to agree with what the Minister of Finance has said, namely, that so far as the main agricultural products for which we expect to have a market in Great Britain are concerned, we have made arrangements which are satisfactory. To suggest from that that we are always going to have a satisfactory arrangement with Great Britain is a question that seems to be in the minds of hon. members.
I say that the arrangements are satisfactory. What we did was to sit down with the British and estimate the amount of our farm products, other than wheat, which they would be required to take in order to leave us without surpluses. Fortunately the position
[Mr Howe.J

at the moment is that we have been able to sell our beef cattle; up until very recently we could have sold our pork products, if necessary; we could have sold most of our dairy products up until very recently in another market, particularly the United States market, at prices which were a little better than we could obtain from the British. But we estimated that on balance throughout the year we would probably be able to sell for about the same price to Britain under the agreements which we made.
Having figured the quantities which we had, and having determined that we could sell certain quantities in other countries, we made agreements with Britain which are taking all the surplus products that we have for sale to Britain. In the case of bacon, we have not been able up to now to fill the contract with Britain. They are taking all the cheese that we can supply, but we have not been able to fill the contract up to the present time. They have been taking all our dried and frozen eggs and we have been selling our fresh eggs in the United States market.
In other words, the negotiations with regard to these products have resulted in the sale of our surpluses. As has been said so often, I do not think that we could improve our position in the British market by going there and saying, "Unless you buy all our surpluses, unless you take them off our hands, in spite of the fact that we can sell some of it elsewhere, we are not going to play with you". That is not the way to establish yourself in a good market.
The British have their difficulties in balancing trade at the present time, as we have ours. What we said to them in effect on our last meeting was: "We are prepared to co-operate with you; we would like to see you putting forth an effort, and we would like to see our friends in the United States putting forth some effort; we would like to see some others who have not had the same difficulties we have had in reaching a balance put forth some effort to assist. We have not ourselves been able to see our way through". I know the suggestion is made that nobody has done anything about it, but the fact is that the products which the British have bought are products that they would have preferred not to have bought at all in order to make their trade balances complete at as early a date as possible.
In spite of the fact that they would have preferred to do that, they have bought our products. I may say to hon. members that they are still negotiating with us to buy our farm products over a long period on a basis similar to that on which they are buying from 29087-104.
Foreign Exchange Control other countries. At no time has Great Britain bought from any other country in the world, so far as I know, on a basis similar to that on which she has bought products in this country.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
The less my hon. friends over in the Conservative corner say about it, the less I will say about their responsibility for the position. The British have been buying our products on a different basis from that on which they are buying other countries' products. They have been agreeing with us year by year down until the last two years to put into the contract a figure which would induce our people to produce more. They have agreed with us to pay a set price for the product and to make the determination of that price official in the agreement from the beginning. Their agreements with other countries have been quite different. They have had a maximum amount that they were prepared to take from those countries, and they have had a minimum amount that those countries were required to deliver. Then in addition they had a provision in the contract whereby they could renegotiate the price from time to time. When there was a possibility of their being able to buy a product in some other country at some other price they were permitted to renegotiate the price downward with the country with which they had the contract.
The difficulties that we have had with the British have not been difficulties of the type that have been in the minds of hon. members who have been talking here. There have been discussions as to whether we should follow the same practice that has been followed with other countries. I have been wondering all through this debate why my hon. friends in the opposition have been making so many inquiries about barter trade. I recall when the chief exponent of barter trade in the Dominion of Canada in 1939 was the last leader of the Progressive Conservative party while he was premier of the province of Manitoba. I am quite satisfied that he could tell them about the negotiations between that province and a certain European country with regard to barter trade.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: Which country?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: I will leave it to the hon. gentleman to say.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: You tell us.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
My hon. friend knows the country; he can tell us what country it was. In any case we have had fairly satisfactory dealings, I would say very satisfactory dealings, with the British. Although we had signed a contract with them to take our surplus beef, when we could get a higher

Foreign Exchange Control price for it in the United States they agreed to our closing out the contract in the middle of the season and selling our beef in the United States. We have had other negotiations from time to time and we have met them in their attempts to balance their own trading with this and other countries by cutting down on the amounts that we expected them to take at any time when we could sell the remainder of the surplus to someone else or at any time our own people were able to consume all or the greater part of what we had. Someone said, what about apples?

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: Honey.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
I dealt with apples on two previous occasions, and I cannot improve upon the reason I gave for the position in Great Britain. My hon. friend, who comes from a country where we used to grow a lot of apples, shakes his head; but if he will look at the records that were quoted the other day he will find that in spite of the fact that an increase in purchases from Australia can be shown, or an increase in the purchases from somewhere else, the British are importing very much less in the way of apples than they were in the early periods that were mentioned. That is due to the fact that they are producing more apples in their own country.
My hon. friends opposite speak of the necessity of getting back to the law of supply and demand. That has been one of their main arguments today, that we should get back to the point where we would be governed by the law of supply and demand, and they say that then the value of our money would take care of itself. Well, the first people in this country to depart from the law of supply and demand were the official opposition when they formed a government under the late Eight Hon. R. B. Bennett. That was back in 1932. The only free trade country in the world, the best market we had for food products, was compelled by them to abandon that policy. Now when these gentlemen come along and say we ought to get back to the law of supply and demand I say to them that the only way we will ever get back to it is to get a Liberal government in Great Britain, as they have in the United States and we have in Canada. Then we will all get back to it.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
The minister answered that part of the queries raised on this side of the house having to do with Britain taking goods from Canada, which I presume was his particular assignment. Many of us here are concerned about why Britain is not sending more goods of a kind we can use here, instead of sending them to other countries, so that in turn Britain would have more Canadian dollars with which to buy more of the particular products with which the minister was 
concerned. Does he have any information to convey to the committee in that regard?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, I am sorry the hon. member does not listen to my speeches; and I am afraid that even if I break the rules of the house and repeat my speech, he still will not listen to it.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
One of your political
speeches.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: My speeches are all political; that is why they are all good. I have never made any excuses for being in politics. I think it is the best job the country offers.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
We all
know you are in politics.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
The question is why the
British find it necessary or advisable to take certain commodities from Poland, Denmark and perhaps some other European countries, with which we could supply them if we were to either ask our own people to eat less or ship them products for which we already have a market elsewhere. Why do they prefer to take those products from some other country and send to that country some things we might like to have? Well, the minister has given the fundamental reason for the present position; the costs in different places. The real basis of the reason, in fact, is that which I gave the house previously, namely that Britain over a period extending back to 1932 has been under contract to take these products from other countries. She was forced into that contract when she was forced off the system of free trade which had been in effect up to that time. She was forced off that policy in 1932 as the result of two elections in Britain in which the people who were in favour of continuing that policy were defeated. Though she was not able to carry out the policy under quotas during the war years, immediately the war was over she resumed it. While Denmark has not been able up to the present to supply the quantity of bacon or the eggs that Britain agreed to take, and while Poland has not been able to supply the amount of bacon Britain agreed to take, I have no doubt that Britain will continue to follow the policy she has always followed, that once she enters into an agreement with anyone that agreement is carried out until a new agreement is made.
The great difficulty in making new agreements at present is the idea which was expressed here today by one hon. member, and which was also expressed back at that time; that is, that for thirty years there have not been any markets of the kind we used to talk about. That statement always sounds rather silly to me, though I was told not to use that word in the house. It does sound

silly, nevertheless, in view of the fact that we have three times the trade now that we had when that statement was made. Our trade has gone up every year since then, so that today it is at least three times what it was when it was said there were no markets to be had in the world.

As far as I am concerned, I think Britain has had the greatest battle of any country in the world, and I think she has made the best job of handling it of any country in the world.

My hon. friend says it was under a socialist government. If the socialist government had not had the plans all laid down previously by a good government, before they came into power, I doubt very much whether within their own ranks they had sufficient strength to evolve the policies which are being put into effect. The British people entered into the war at the peak of their influence among the nations of the world, financially and otherwise. They did not ask help from anybody. They said, "We think we are right, and we are proceeding to demonstrate that we think we are right."
This is not the first time Britain has done that. Britain has done that five times in the last three centuries. The only reason that Britain has been supported by ourselves and other countries is the fact that we, too, were convinced she was right. She carried on on that basis for at least one-third of this war and for the greater period of the first war

Britain went through both of these wars and we went through with her. It is not more than eighteen months ago when everyone I met who came back from Great Britain was saying, "Britain is through." I used to turn on the radio night after night and hear messages broadcast from the other side of the line to the effect that Britain was on the way out. I want to say, to those who are talking so much about communism now, that those were communistic messages. Britain was not on the way out. I took in my hands my own position as a possible prophet and declared that within five years Britain would be restored to her financial position among the nations of the world; that she would be trading with the other countries in much the same way as she traded before.
So far as I am concerned, I am prepared to do everything and to assist the government in doing everything possible in order to put Britain back into that position. I do not care what country you are talking about, there is no country in the world-I do not exempt any country from that statement-that has done more to establish world peace than Great Britain. She has done so by creating in the world the commonwealth of nations to which we belong. I think our first duty in Canada is to see to it that when we are all through with this scrap about money-I am not going to try to lay the blame for it-the one nation that has done more to maintain peace than any other nation, no matter what political party she has been under, ought to be supported.
If by selling her less food for a year or two. and selling the rest of our surplus somewhere else, or even persuading our own people to eat it, we are going to help her resume her position, then, Mr. Chairman, I think we ought to do it. Someone mentioned honey. The honey producers were in to see me yesterday. We have been advertising honey in Canada to get the people to eat it, and they are eating it. If the Canadian people continue to eat it in the quantities they naturally should, we will not have any problem in getting rid of our honey. It may do us a lot of good to eat it.
Some of our other problems are in a similar position. In the house there has been an overemphasis on the problem of getting rid of our food products. Our food products are going out at fairly good returns and we are hopeful we may be able to maintain that position.

I think it is true to say generally that there have been many things produced in Great Britain and exported to soft currency countries which could have been sent to Canada. Can the Minister of Finance throw any light upon that-before I ask further questions?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: I had intended at another time, and still intend, to deal in somewhat greater detail with the question the hon. member has raised. Generally speaking, however, I can say this-

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: Would the minister prefer to answer it at another time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
I would, because I do not have figures with me. However, perhaps I could give a general answer at this time-and I am sure this will be concurred in by my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
When the chancellor was here last September we urged upon him strongly the desirability of endeavouring to persuade British exporters to direct as much of their production as possible to the Canadian market. As members of the committee are aware, we have been particularly interested in textiles because, prior to the war, British textiles were exported in substantial quantities to this country. As a result of the war that market was largely taken over by American exports-Canadian imports from the United States.
As a result of the severe import restrictions against the United States there was a great opportunity for British textile manufacturers to export to this country, and they have been doing so in fairly substantial volume. When Sir Raymond Streit, chairman of the textile group, was out here-he has been here on several occasions-great stress was laid upon the desirability of directing

as many exports as possible to Canada. Substantial success has been achieved along those lines, although not as great as we would have wished.
I am not familiar with all the details; but I do know that my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce, as a result of discussions with board of trade people in the United Kingdom, was able to arrange for a substantial divergence of steel to Canada. The joint committee which was set up following the chancellor's visit met in London a month or so ago; and again at those meetings we impressed upon the British government-at official levels, it is true-our anxiety that everything should be done to encourage exports of this type from the United Kingdom. I propose to deal with some aspects of the matter at greater length, perhaps in my budget speech. I have no doubt that the Minister of Trade and Commerce will be doing so, too.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: The annual report of the foreign exchange control board points out that official holdings of gold and United States dollars increased by $496 million. May I ask the minister if the amount of United States currency which Canada would have received through the purchase of a minority interest in the International Petroleum Company by Standard Oil of New Jersey would be reflected in the 1948 account, or would it be reflected in the 1949 account; and approximately how much in millions of dollars would it be?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: I would have to check on that. I should, think it would likely be reflected in the 1948 accounts. I am afraid, however, that I could not give an accurate answer, but I shall get the information and give it to the hon. member at the next stage.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
May I ask how this $496 million of very valuable assets now held by the Bank of Canada is paid for? I presume it is with Canadian dollars. It would make a difference in the budget surplus as shown in cash surplus, when the minister gives us the nation's accounts next Tuesday night. However, I do not wish to anticipate his statement to be made at that time. What will be the government's policy in regard to allowing Canadians to reinstate to some extent their capital position with regard to American securities? The minister will recall how valuable it was for Canada to be able to put our hands on American securities in the possession of Canadian individuals and companies. Some of those securities were not at that time taken over by the government; but in many cases individuals and companies sold part or all of their American securities, and the money went to provide very necessary

funds to purchase munitions in the United States before that country came into the war.
Would it be against the policy of the government to allow Canadian individuals to repurchase American securities? Those securities of course would be under the jurisdiction of the foreign exchange control board. This would allow Canadians a certain amount of freedom which they would not have otherwise.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: So far no consideration has been given to changing the existing policy which, generally speaking, does not allow Canadians to obtain United States dollars for the purpose of investing in American securities.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: May I ask if there is any reason for continuing that policy, or is it just like so many things which have found their way to the statute books? They are never removed because the bureaucrats have not found it necessary to remove them, and the public do not make a big enough fuss.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: The reason is that the government does not consider our reserve position is as yet sufficient to permit us to allow our store of United States dollars to be used to purchase American securities, which would naturally be subject to market fluctuations- to which currency and gold are not subject.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
With regard to what was so clearly and ably said by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, the minister should keep in mind that at the time of the Bretton Woods agreement, after the impasse between the British proposals and those made by Mr. White on behalf of the United States, it was Canada that took the lead, and it was the Canadian compromise proposal which was finally accepted.
Canada took the lead at that time, and I submit she could now take the lead again in asking that the international monetary fund go into the matter we are now discussing, to see if the regulations could not be altered so that the greatly desirable quality of convertibility might be returned to the currencies of the world.
No one realizes more than I what a stupendous task it would be. But I wish to tell the committee and the minister that Canada did take the lead in overcoming the impasse between the United States and Great Britain at the time of the Bretton Woods agreement; it was our proposal which was finally accepted. I believe we could again take the lead.
I suggested last night, as I have done repeatedly, that an initial step would be the establishment of a free gold market so that we could have some common denominator to
Foreign Exchange Control which we could relate our currencies. I shall not labour the point now. I did mention however that there is a considerable body of support for that contention in both the United States and Canada. I believe it should be explored a good deal further. The minister said-and in error I suggest-that the United States dollar was the only currency not subject to exchange control.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: I should have included the Swiss.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
The Swiss is the only currency that is really not subject to exchange control. The United States dollar is subject to the most rigid exchange control in that the holders are not allowed to convert into gold. The gold exchange act of the United States specifically prohibits the purchase of gold with United States dollars. Unless that quality is returned to a currency you cannot say that that currency is free of exchange control.
I should like to quote one thing in connection with this matter of purchases in Great Britain. What the Minister of Agriculture said about this was most interesting. He, like myself, believes that convertibility is essential, that we must do everything we can to strive for that. We owe to the United Kingdom, in fact all civilization owes, a debt that probably can never be repaid. Without the United Kingdom we would probably still be engaged in hostilities or be a vassal state. This is what Mr. Elliott M. Little had to say, as reported in a Reuters dispatch from London in today's Ottawa Journal:
"We are not satisfied that everything possible is being done by you or by ourselves to overcome this dollar problem". Little declared in a speech at the annual dinner of the Paper Makers Association of Great Britain and Ireland.
"It is not only Canada's pulp and paper trade with Britain which has been affected by the exchange problem", Little asserted.
"In the past year one traditional market after another has been reduced or has disappeared and old customers for Canadian pulp and paper products have turned to other countries at much higher prices or have gone without supplies they wished to have."
Granted that the bulk of our newsprint goes to the United States, the fact is that the United Kingdom has been a traditional market for a major part of our production of wood pulp and newsprint. But we find United Kingdom buyers of wood pulp and newsprint paying higher prices for an inferior newsprint in other soft currency countries. Everything should be done to overcome that problem. For the Minister of Finance to stand up and say that it is an impossible problem is not taking a realistic view of the situation.
1648	HOUSE OF
Transitional Measures Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: I have not said that it is impossible.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
Pretty nearly. We have to be prepared to take a chance; we have to be prepared to take courageous action. If we do not, there will be more and more articles such as this appearing in the press.
Despite the fact that our export trade last year was at a record level, the situation is so ominous that I believe the government has no time to lose in taking steps. I have suggested that the thing to do is to go to the international monetary fund and see if some new arrangement cannot be made to allow- perhaps only in small quantities to start with, perhaps only in a minor scale-these currencies to be given the essential quality of free convertibility.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in, on division. Mr. Abbott thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 85, to amend the Foreign Exchange Control Act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speakerposition: topic
Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
At seven-thirty we will proceed in committee with the resolution in the name of the Minister of Justice dealing with emergency powers.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at seven-thirty o'clock.

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The house resumed from Wednesday, March 16, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Garson-Mr. Golding in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the continuation of certain orders and regulations of the governor in council for a limited period during the national emergency arising out of the war.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the committee requires a good deal of information before this resolution can be reported back to the house. It is also information the house should have before it undertakes to debate the principle of the bill that may follow, when second reading is moved. It is with a view to eliciting that essential information that I should like to put a number of questions to the Minister of Justice. I think I have made it clear that I regard this as


essential information, and that the purpose of these questions is to ascertain facts which are highly important both in regard to the validity of the measure that will follow and also as to particular aspects of it. The minister did furnish certain information when he spoke in the house on March 15, but there is still quite an area in which I do not think the information before the house is adequate.
We have been told that certain orders, twelve in all, will be continued by this bill. Enough has been said by the minister, I think, to indicate that the bill will contemplate continuation of the orders in their present form. In the first place I wish the minister would be good enough to tell us something further about the orders. When he spoke last Wednesday he enumerated the twelve orders, of which I find six were amended by the statute itself in 1947. The legislation of 1947 actually contained amendments to those six orders, and section 4 of that statute does not permit the governor in council to do anything but revoke orders in whole or in part; there is no power of amendment. However, intimations have been given by members of the government at one time or another that certain amendments are being made, and I wonder if the minister would indicate just how that is being done.
Let me illustrate. When the Minister of Finance spoke on this subject on February 7, I am afraid altogether too briefly, he indicated that the bill would confine the effect of price control to some dozen or so commodities which he listed. That list is on pages 316 and 317 of Hansard. That would involve some provision in the statute, I should think, and I wonder if the minister would indicate just how that would be brought about. Another change was also intimated by the Minister of Finance on another occasion, when he said it would be the purpose to amend the general order in relation to the powers of the wartime prices and trade board so that, without indicating just how it would be done, the effect would be to amend section 8 of that general order by eliminating the "reasonable and just" provision in relation to price control.
That is one subject of inquiry, namely how these changes have been brought about. Perhaps I might stop here and give the minister an opportunity to reply.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Section 4 of the 1947 act enables the governor in council only to revoke but not to amend the orders in council, and my hon. friend's first question is how those orders may be amended in view of that provision. I apprehend that they will be amended as part of the schedule of the bill we are now seeking to amend by the

legislation which will be found on the resolution now before us. I regret that I did not have the opportunity of being in the house or in charge of this measure at the time the 1947 act was passed, but I think I am right in saying that the amendments on that occasion were part of the bill itself. In view of the fact that the governor in council has no power to amend, the only way an amendment could be made would be by means of the present bill in its passage through the house.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Does the bill now make that provision?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No; it does not. We went on the assumption that these orders in council having been considered item by item and oi'der by order in 1947, when the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act was passed and, as I am informed, having been considered order by order in 1948, when that amendment was passed-

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Not in 1948.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
That is my information from the gentleman who attended the committee. It may be that my hon. friend's recollection is different; however, nothing turns on that. But having been considered in 1947 and, as I contend, again in 1948, our thought was that the orders in council would be regarded as acceptable in their present form by a majority of the members. If they are not so regarded, then I imagine it would be open to the house to further amend them in much the same way that this was done in the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act, 1947. Speaking from recollection, I do not think there is any provision in this bill for the amendment of the orders in council in the schedule.
I believe they are indicated there as having been amended by the 1947 act. However, I do not think any difficulty would arise in that regard if it were the desire of a majority of hon. members to have an amendment; I think the only problem would be one of draftsmanship.
With regard to my hon. friend's second question, I am rather in a predicament in trying to answer it without referring to one of the sections of the bill. Exception was taken in the house the other day when I did this, but perhaps hon. members will not object if I read section 2 of the bill we will be introducing if this resolution carries:
Notwithstanding anything in the said act or in any order or regulation set out in the schedule thereto, the wartime prices and trade board shall not,
(b) -
This is the point my hon. friend was inquiring about.
-grant leave to prosecute any person for violation of subsection one of section eight of the wartime
Transitional Measures Act prices and trade board regulations with respect to any goods or services other than the goods and services with respect to which an order of the board was made under that paragraph and is In force at the commencement of this act.
By the way, my hon. friend, I think, will recognize subsection one of section eight of the regulations-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I do not believe it would be in order to deal with those sections of the bill at the present time.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The minister could state the effect of the section without actually giving a verbatim rendering.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I have already offended the rule and given a verbatim report of the section which will answer my hon. friend's question. I am now referring not to the bill which is being introduced, but to subsection 1 of section 8 of the actual regulations which are in force under the old statute. This is the subsection which provides that:
No person shall sell or offer for sale or supply goods or services at a price that is higher than reasonable and just-

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
My next question has to do with the emergency which must exist if this legislation is to have any validity. I think the house will wish to be assured it is not passing legislation that is likely to be challenged and upset in the courts. Having regard to the fact, as was pointed out in the house on Tuesday, that there is a great deal of breadth to these orders, more than is required now in relation to the field in which the orders are to operate as compared with the original field, I think the minister will appreciate that if we legislate more broadly than is required to cover the field within which a national emergency is said to exist we are simply laying the legislation open to attack as being ultra vires. We will have to keep our legislation within the ambit of a national emergency. I should like the minister, if he will, to indicate in what respect the emergency may today be said to exist with regard to some matters that are covered by the general order which one might well call the mother order, P.C. 8528. This is the order that clothes the wartime prices and trade board with its broadest powers.
For instance, this order not only gives power to the wartime prices and trade board to fix prices, but it also gives the board power to fix the return on services. If you look at the definition of services you will see that, if this order is continued, the wartime prices and trade board will have the power to determine the remuneration-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
To what page is my hon. friend referring?
1650	HOUSE OF
Transitional Measures Act

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I am referring to P.C. 8528, page 20 of the consolidation that was used in 1947. You will see that services include the following specific services and any activities or undertakings associated therewith or ancillary thereto, and also any activities or undertakings that may hereafter be designated by the board as services for the purposes of these regulations. The first service mentioned is the transportation of goods.
Now, I think the minister must tell the house wherein a national emergency exists in Canada today with respect to the transportation of goods, warehousing and storage.
I think he must tell us the same thing with regard to laundering and cleaning; tailoring and dressmaking; hairdressing and beauty parlour services; the supplying of meals; refreshments and beverages; the renting and and exhibiting of moving pictures; manufacturing processes performed on a custom or commission basis; the dyeing of furs; the dressing of furs; the slaughtering or dressing of animals or poultry on a custom or commission basis; the breaking and separating of eggs on a custom or commission basis; the pasteurizing of honey on a custom or commission basis; the drying of any goods on a custom or commission basis; the packing or packaging of any goods on a custom or commission basis.
Then further powers are given to the board with respect to putting a price on services, quite apart from goods. Now that is not the only feature in which the proposed extent of the order or, for that matter, the full extent of the order today has not been exercised; that power is not being exercised today by the board. The board's orders do not extend to the fixing of a price for services of that kind any more than they extend to the fixing of the price of goods other than those dozen commodities which appear at page 316 of Hansard.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: This discussion is entirely concerned with the contents of the bill and has nothing to do with the resolution. Surely we cannot discuss the bill when the bill is not before us.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: If the minister will wait, he will see the point to which this question is directed.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I have waited quite a while.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I do not care whether or not the minister is getting itchy. At the moment,
I am trying to get some information which the house ought to have before it gives second reading to the bill. The house will not have that information unless it gets it here, at this stage. This is the purpose of the resolution stage in committee, in order that members
'Mr. Garson.]

may secure information which would enable them to use their intelligence in deciding how they should vote when the bill is presented.
I pointed out that there is a particular provision in the order in council to which I have referred, and there are others to which I could refer as well which are outside the scope of the regulations now being enforced by the board. I am not asking the minister to disclose the contents of the bill, but I wish he would state clearly how it is proposed to deal with this question so that the house may be sure that what is to follow is not going to have the effect of keeping alive a power with respect to matters on which the board has power today by these orders, but concerning which there surely cannot be said to be a national emergency today.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I must disagree with my hon. friend in his proposition that, in order to found a jurisdiction of this parliament to pass a law such as the bill we are seeking in this resolution, it must be founded upon an emergency in respect of, we will say, the transportation of goods, or warehouse and storage. I apprehend that, once a national emergency has been established, then, on the basis of that national emergency, parliament can legislate with regard to any of those matters if it so chooses. My hon. friend's objection is not, therefore, well taken in so far as the question of jurisdiction is concerned.
It is perhaps well taken, although I did not understand him to address himself to that point, to the matter that under the present conditions, he might argue there is no longer the necessity to regulate these particular matters. Now, I do not think he can anticipate the bill by making that assumption, even though I have disclosed to him part of the contents of section 2 of the bill. I would suggest that by far the most practical way of dealing with the difficulty which is bothering my hon. friend is to proceed with this present stage; then when the bill is in the committee stage, we can have those who are charged with its administration before the committee of the house. Then we can explain to my hon. friend, I hope to his satisfaction, just wherein arises the necessity for these particular provisions that he has been reading.
As to the jurisdiction aspect of the matter, in drafting the bill our law officers have satisfied themselves upon that score; and with all deference I think that the problem to which my hon. friend alludes does not arise.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman suggest that this bill is going to a private committee and is not to be dealt with in the house?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No. We shall bring it into the committee of the whole.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: But we are not going to hear witnesses in the committee of the whole, are we? It is not the practice to hear witnesses before this committee of the whole.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No, I understand not. I am somewhat at a disadvantage, in this respect, I must admit, because this is the first session in which I have been in this chamber. But I understand that the practice is that the various ministers may have officials of their departments attend with them in this house, and that, when a question is asked of the minister, he informs himself from his officials and relays the information to the house.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The minister is quite right as regards matters of detail, I was going to say. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, for instance, has a number of gentlemen come at different times to give him figures about trade and such matters. But we are now dealing with a question of principle. I was going to ask the minister if he could inform the house what are the elements that constitute the national emergency upon which he relies.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I certainly have never held myself out to be an expert upon national emergencies, and I would question if even an expert could give a comprehensive and completely satisfactory definition. But I do not think that is necessary in the case before us because, as I said the other day in my remarks when I was speaking on the motion to go into committee, the economic emergency with which this country has been continuously faced since the cessation of hostilities is one which I think the members of this house were quite right in affirming as existing, by a vote of some 141 to 53. For the purpose we have here, that of making a foundation for our jurisdiction to pass this bill, I think that all we have to do is to satisfy a majority of the members of this parliament. Then you have an emergency which is sufficient for the purposes of founding jurisdiction to pass the bill. I am not raising this as any point of order at all. That is a matter that has already been determined.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: With great deference, may I say that the question of emergency is one of fact.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
It is not a question of what I or somebody else might think about it. At this juncture I think this question becomes a matter of grave importance, because the mere declaration of an emergency does not create
Transitional Measures Act one. If there be enacted legislation founded upon an assumption which the facts contradict, the minister will agree with me that great hardship may ensue; because we are a law-abiding people and we shall observe the law even while resisting it.
Without being too specific, the minister coming from Manitoba will know what I mean when I say that a high authority, confirmed by still higher authority, after hearing witnesses who testified on a broad range of topics, has said that not only is there no national emergency but that there never has been a time when we were more remote from an emergency than we are today. In fact, should I by chance, good or ill, find myself on the other side of the house, I might be inclined to welcome that document as a testimonial to the efficiency of the government in power. But the fact remains that, by a body before whom we as law-abiding people incline, it has been held that there is no national emergency. As prudent and careful men who seek to protect the interests of the country at large, I think there should be some reluctance on the part of parliament to enact legislation which in all probability-and I say "in all probability" because of the. elements that point that way-will be ill founded in fact. I ask the hon. gentleman this question. What has happened since last Thursday or a week ago yesterday which prompts him to say that today a national emergency exists, when a week ago it was declared by a high authority that there was no such emergency?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I think that my friend's argument is founded upon a fallacy, if I may say so; and the fallacy is this. Merely because the Manitoba court of appeal, as some of a group of five men in Canada, finds as a matter of fact that there is no national emergency does not extinguish the fact, if the fact exists. So far as I am personally concerned, notwithstanding the testimonial aspect of their findings, I am myself in the most profound disagreement with this finding of facts. My hon. friend says, and rightly so, that this is a question of fact. But facts, for the purpose of founding jurisdiction in a case of this sort, are something that groups of people must find. They must find them to be facts. Human error being what it is, it is inevitable that some groups will find a thing to be a fact and another group will find that it is not a fact. I might say with just as much force as has my hon. friend that-I think it was yesterday or the day before-this parliament by a vote of 141 to 53, found that there was an emergency in Canada. I claim for the finding of this highest court in the land at least as much validity as my hon. friend can claim for certain members of the Manitoba

Transitional Measures Act court of appeal. Without attempting to discuss a matter which is, I think, for all practical purposes sub judice, I may tell him that we do not agree at all with the judgment of the Manitoba court of appeal either with regard to some of its findings of fact or with regard to some of the legal principles that it has invoked. We intend to appeal that case. The case is by no means ended. There as yet has not been in that case a final and ultimate finding which will carry the force of law, because we can appeal it, and we intend to appeal it. Not until after that appeal has been disposed of will my hon. friend be in a position to inVoke it in support of his contention that there is no emergency existing in Canada today.
I do not want to repeat the argument which I made in the house, when I moved that the Speaker do leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of the whole to consider this resolution, as to the reason which I stated for there being an emergency in Canada at the present time, because I do not think it is fair to bore hon. members by quoting from one's own speeches. I am sure that what I said is fresh in the minds of those who paid any attention to it in the first place. But even if my hon. friend objects to my remarks as not being correct statements of fact-and I think he would have great difficulty in doing so, because they were all so self-evident as to be platitudinous-I would ask him to look about him if he wishes to see proof of there being an emergency in Canada and listen to the remarks of his colleagues, the hon. member for Danforth, the hon. member for Davenport, the hon. member for Rose-dale, the hon. member for York West and the hon. member for York South, who, during the last two days, have given the most excellent statements in great detail of various aspects of this emergency.
The leader of the opposition himself says that, although his party voted against the resolution which would lead to the introduction of rent control, neither he nor his party have declared themselves to be not in favour of rent control. They are in favour of rent control-for what reason? Because there is an emergency. If there is no emergency there is no need for rent control.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Will the minister permit a question? Is it not a fact that the leader of the opposition pointed to specific rather than general emergencies? Is the minister not suggesting that there is a general emergency?
