maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Indeed I am, sir. I do not know how the idea got about that specific emergencies are necessary as the foundation of the jurisdiction of this parliament.
fMr. Garson.]

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I doubt very much whether anybody alleges that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I agree with my hon. friend that no person alleges it, but many people alluded to it. The hon. member for Nanaimo himself seems to be under that illusion.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I do not think so.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Let us be perfectly fair. Are my hon. friends of the Progressive Conservative party and I in agreement that all that is necessary is a general emergency for the foundation of our jurisdiction to pass the proposed bill?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: On a question of privilege, I have never referred to anything which would lead the minister to make such a statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. He is quite right in the point he has raised. I meant to refer to the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, who has just made that statement. My hon. friend from Nanaimo is quite right.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Will the minister permit a question from this corner of the house? If he says that there is a general emergency, as he is arguing, why are we dropping so many controls as he proposes to do?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is a very easy question to answer, Mr. Chairman. While the general emergency is the foundation for the jurisdiction that we propose to exercise here, it is a matter of judgment in dealing with the general emergency as to how we should carry on controls or dispense with them.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The judgment has not been very good in the past.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: While my hon. friend may not agree with the judgment we have exercised, yet we happen to be in charge of the affairs of the government and that is what we thought to be the proper course to follow. Probably I have dealt with the points raised.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It was not their parliament.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It was a parliament which enacted legislation which was binding upon them, and it was against those enactments that they rebelled.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Because they had no representation.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am not going to deal with side issues. I say that the American colonies rebelled against an omnipotent parliament; and there grew up on this continent a new form of government, a form of government which, instead of being an omnipotent government, depended for its efficacy and its operation upon a system of checks and balances. In the United States there was the legislative power.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend if he is now dealing with the United States constitution?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I am dealing with ours. For the moment I am referring to the United States constitution but I am coming to ours. I was going to say that in the United States the powers were divided into three: the legislative, the executive and the judicial. The supreme court of the United States was given the power to determine whether or not the laws enacted by Congress were constitutional, were binding; that is, whether or not legislation passed by the legislative body was effective, and could be applied to an individual. Some ninety years later another group of North American colonies set up another union which again refuted the doctrine of an omnipotent parliament; Canada, in a way all her own, devised a method of checks and balances. It was different from the United States system because Canada still retained the king. But our system followed the United States system to the extent that we had a constitution, although it happened to be a statute enacted by the British parliament. Any law enacted by the Canadian parliament or by a legislature of a Canadian province is valid only in so far as the lawmaker can point to the chapter and verse in the constitution which gives him authority to enact that law. And the arbiter upon whom was placed the duty of determining whether or not a law is constitutional and binding is the judiciary, the courts of the land-the trial courts, the courts of appeal and, in the early days, the privy council, because there was no supreme court
Transitional Measures Act until 1875, and after that date the Supreme Court of Canada and the privy council.
I think my hon. friend will admit that there is a presumption that a judgment is right. There are courts of appeal for the purpose of correcting error. But my hon. friend will admit also, I am sure, that in ordinary cases a judgment of a court, especially a court presided over by an able and experienced judge, which has been unanimously confirmed by the highest court of a province-and when, be it remarked, the confirmation deals with a fact-permits of no successful appeal. I am not saying that in this instance an appeal may not succeed. But in the ordinary instance, in the ordinary case, I am sure my hon. friend will admit there is but scant hope for the success of an appeal from a case on which there have been two concurrent findings of fact.
In the case about which we are talking, the question was this: Is there an emergency? Because it is only if and when there is an emergency that the powers which give vigour and force and life to the order in council, and to the statute under which it is passed, exist. It has been held by a trial court, it has been held by a court of appeal in respect of this simple question of fact, that there is no national emergency, and that in consequence-

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Certainly.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Do I understand that the hon. member for Stanstead contends it was the unanimous finding of the court of appeal of Manitoba, in the judgment to which he referred, that there was no national emergency? If he answers yes to that question, then I would ask him if he has read the judgment. I have it here. He should be careful.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I was saying that there has been a finding of fact.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: By one judge out of five.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I was saying there had been a finding of fact in the trial court, and that the court of appeal has confirmed that judgment and has confirmed it on the facts. I submit to the minister that while I believe most of us would be loath in an ordinary case-and this is not an ordinary case-to advise an appeal to a higher tribunal where there has been a concurrent finding of fact, there may be reason to appeal here. In fact, I would expect there would be an appeal in a matter of this importance.

Transitional Measures Act
But, all that being so, does it not impose upon the government at this juncture, before enacting more legislation which is subject to challenge and which, if successfully challenged, may cause great damage and hardship to a number of people, the duty of giving most careful study to the basis of the alleged emergency.
As the minister knows, there have been several other judgments in which it has been held that no national emergency exists, and the law has in consequence not been susceptible of enforcement. I suggest to the ministry that it is only prudent to state carefully what, in the view of the administration, constitutes a national emergency, and endeavour to ascertain if the facts, which are probably known to most of us, are such that it can be safely declared that a national emergency exists.
I do not wish to be facetious; and in matters of this kind which create great perplexities, I do not wish to be unduly partisan. I feel there is too much at stake to attempt to secure any political advantage or party advantage in a matter of this kind. But where are we going to find evidence of an emergency? I will admit-and I hope my hon. friend will not take it amiss-that there is a political crisis. I will admit that a government which, in its everyday activities, is relatively strong but which, in fact, compared to the entire opposition, is not so, finds itself in a difficult position. And I believe in a matter of this kind and of this importance parliament should go slowly. We should inquire with care and with the utmost scru'iny into the elements upon which the government relies to constitute this a national emergency.
To most of us a national emergency means national peril. It means the type of thing which arises when the enemy is at the gate. But anything in the way of an inconvenience, anything in the way of a local disturbance or turbulence, does not, I submit, according to the authorities and according to popular understanding, constitute a national emergency.
Then I say to the hon. member for Mont-magny-L'Islet that I too have the judgment of the court of appeal of Manitoba. And while I do not take the same view of it that he does, let me assure him that I too have read it carefully, and I hope my powers of comprehension have not abandoned me.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I should like to quote from the judgment of Mr. Justice Dysart, and ask' the hon. member for Stanstead if he can find anything that even resembles a declaration
IMr Haekett.l
in those reasons for judgment that there is no national emergency. The judgment states:
The act-
And he was speaking about the transitional powers act-
-clearly invades the field of ''property and civil rights" which, by the British North America Act, section 92(13) are committed to the provincial legislatures. But the parliament of the dominion in a sufficiently great emergency, such as that arising out of war, has power to deal adequately with that emergency for the safety of the dominion as a whole.
The interests of the dominion are to be protected, and it rests with the parliament of the dominion to protect them. What those interests are the parliament of the dominion must be left with considerable freedom to judge; per Lord Wright, in Co-operative Committee on Japanese Canadians v. Attorney General for Canada, 1947 A.C. 87 at 101.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am reading the judgment.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The hon. gentleman knows that Mr. Justice Dysart did not dissent from the judgment which confirmed the judgment of the chief justice.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am about to read his reasons.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: His conclusion was that the appeal should be dismissed.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Of course, and I am about to read the reason he gave for concluding that. A little later on in his notes he says: Parliament has declared that the emergency is still continuing. That declaration is peculiarly within the rights of parliament to make. And although the judiciary has the right, in a proper case, to review parliament's decision, and has a duty, upon sufficient evidence, to reverse that decision, still the courts ought not to venture upon such a review or reversal unless the need of doing so is clear. The courts have always exercised that right "with reluctance"; per Lord Haldane in In re the Board of Commerce Act, 1919, and the Combines and Fair Prices Act, 1919, reported in 1922, 1 A.C. 191 at 200.
That is the very question we have before us, whether there is an emergency or not. The judgment goes on:
In my view, P.C. 1292 goes beyond the act, and to the extent of that excess is invalid. That view renders it unnecessary-and I think inadvisable-for me to deal with the validity or invalidity of the transitional act.
Was there concurrence in the expressed opinion of one judge who said that there was no emergency? There is an emergency in Canada at the present time arising out of the last war that is still continuing.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The first war or the second?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Of course the emergency following the first war was of a special kind due to the policies of the Torv government that

we had from 1914 to 1918. The policies of the government during the last war-

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: This time?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I would ask hon. members to refrain from interrupting the speaker, no matter on what side of the house he may sit.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I like it.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Order. Every hon. member should have the opportunity to present his views without interruption. I appeal to hon. members to support the rules by trying to keep proper order and decorum.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: What is an emergency? According to the Oxford dictionary an emergency is a sudden juncture demanding immediate action. Will any hon. member on the other side of the house say that the situation in regard to rents is such that we should do away with it?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Who wants to?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Is there a disturbance or peculiar situation amounting to an emergency in connection with housing? Is that emergency continuing owing to the fact that we were not able to build houses during the war? Is there not an emergency that we should deal with? The leader of the opposition has said that there is. If there is such an emergency why do hon. members on the other side rise in their places from time to time and ask that they be given an example of the emergency? Who will say that the situation with regard to housing is not a national emergency? Will any hon. member rise in his place and say that because of the shortage of certain commodities it is not necessary to keep certain prices down by price control, at least for some time?
If the Tories want to take the responsibility of disrupting the Canadian economy by doing away with all controls at this time let them do so. They must accept that responsibility before the people at the next election and I am mighty glad that they are doing it.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The hon. member has been emphasizing rent control but I ask him to name quickly three other emergencies. Will he stop harping on rent control and name three others? Go ahead. He cannot do it.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The hon. member has only to
read-

speechtext: Answer the question.

speechtext: -the list of twelve orders in council which will be mentioned in the bill and he will have his answer. There are not only three; there are twelve.

speechtext:
Mention them
Transitional Measures Act

speechtext:
For example, steel and distribution of building materials which are in short supply. As I say, if the members of the opposition want to disturb the Canadian economy at this time, let them do so; but they will be responsible to the Canadian people.
I am glad they are taking this stand because it is going to help us and there will be fewer members on the other side after the next election.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I have listened for hours on end to the legal aspects of this argument and I resolved long ago that I would not get into it. After all, it is the sort of situation into which only lawyers would jump. I received through the mail today a copy of the judgment which has been referred to so often during the course of this debate. I also received many other letters in today's mail, to one of which I wish to make reference in a few minutes. This made me decide to say a few words on this legal point. I must admit that the hon. member for Montmagny-L'lslet has said much of what I intended to say, but perhaps not being a lawyer I can express myself in a layman's terms.
I have read to the best of my non-legal ability the judgments of Mr. Justice McPherson, Mr. Justice Coyne, Mr. Justice Dysart and Mr. Justice Adamson of the Manitoba court of appeal. As I read those judgments it seemed to me that there was one thing on which the four justices were agreed, namely, that they were ruling on the validity of order in council P.C. 1292 under the terms of the Transitional Measures Act. They did not rule that the Transitional Measures Act was ultra vires of this parliament, but they did rule that P.C. 1292 was ultra vires of the Transitional Measures Act. I may say by way of digression that I cannot follow their views on that matter. They speak about this 28J cents per bushel that was taken from this man Nolan who held this barley as though he had created that value. As a matter of fact that 28J cents was a fortuitous profit created by the action of the government in removing the ceilings, so to me their argument is very dubious on that point. But that is not the issue now. The issue is clear, and all the legal gentlemen of the official opposition should not keep dragging out these four judgments together with the previous judgment of Mr. Justice Williams as a proof, somehow, that we are doing something here that we have no right to do. The judgments either do not discuss it at all or they admit the validity of the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act itself. The only thing they say is that the act did not give the government power to pass P.C. 1292, because

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
That may be their view, but most farmers in western Canada, who lost heavily and saw others making fortuitous profits because of what happened, do think there was an emergency as far as they were concerned.
I want to leave it at that because, as I said,
I have tried to put it in layman's language, and if I went on I would make it as confusing as most of the lawyers have made it. I said there was another letter I had received. I received this letter in the mail today, and I received as well this document of many pages, in which their lordships say something which makes it possible for the hon. member for Stanstead and others to argue that there is no emergency. maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I do not intend to speak for very long, and I have not read any of the judgments referred to; I have only listened 

to my hon. and learned friend from Stanstead, who spoke of the judgments that had been given in respect to the emergency powers. The hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet mentioned the definition of an emergency. It includes an immediate element not imputable only to war, as the hon. member for Stanstead has said, but arising from unforeseen circumstances. The hon. gentleman spoke at great length about the various acts. He is against controls; he considers them a poison, and the action of the courts as the antidote. Well, the more he insists upon it the less dangerous become the controls, because as long as there is an antidote-I mean the courts-to correct the so-called wrong effect of the controls, how can he complain so much about it? That is all I want to ask him.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I think one or two aspects of this subject need to be clarified. There has been a good deal of discussion, but it seems the further it goes the greater is the attempt on the other side to becloud the issue as we on this side have stated it. That issue was stated in crystal-clear terms by my leader on Wednesday last with regard to this subject of emergency. He pointed out the dangers of the course the government is pursuing, dangers which are revived by the reasons assigned by the Minister of Justice in what he has said tonight.
What my leader said, and what others speaking from this part of the house have said, is that with respect to the housing situation in Canada emergent conditions do exist, and that is the source of the relationship of rent control to this question. We have emergent conditions with respect to housing; we have a crisis in housing. But, Mr. Chairman, to justify a measure which will deal with rent and several other subjects that have been mentioned, the government proposes that this parliament go on record as asserting the existence of a national emergency.
See where that leads us. The minister has said that parliament-I think he means this house-by its vote on Wednesday last asserted the existence of a national emergency. I entirely take issue with that statement. All the house did last Wednesday was to pass a motion that on this particular resolution the house should resolve itself into committee of the whole. It still remains for parliament, and even for this house, to say in binding terms that a national emergency exists. I point out to the Minister of Justice that the measure of 1947 did not put parliament on record in specific terms as asserting the existence of a national emergency. That was in 1947, when we were asked to say that a national emergency required the statutory enactment of fifty-seven orders in council.

All that was done in the act of 1947, which is chapter 16, was to make a reference to it in the preamble. Parliament has not yet asserted in categorical terms, and did not assert in 1947, that there was a national emergency.
For the sake of argument, however, let us say that the recital in the preamble is equivalent to such an assertion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: How much more categorically could parliament make a statement of the emergency in the act of 1947 than to recite that as the fact upon which the exercise of their jurisdiction was based?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The answer is obvious. Parliament can set out a declaration that the emergency does exist. All parliament did in the preamble to the 1947 act was to say that in view of the continuation of the national emergency, and whereas the national emergency in certain respects is continuing, and so on.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: And is still continuing.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
All right; that is a preamble. Even if we were to accept the contention of the minister that a reference of that kind in the preamble is equivalent to the assertion of the existence of a national emergency, I point out that this was in 1947, and parliament has not yet said anything in 1949 by way of a final declaration on this subject.
That leads me to make a comment on the grounds on which the minister proposes to invite parliament, at some stage or other, to assert the existence of a national emergency. He was invited to indicate the evidence by which he says a national emergency exists of a general character. At the moment we are not arguing whether an emergent condition on a national scale exists with respect to housing. Let us not spend any more time threshing old straw there. The minister is asserting the existence of a national emergency. Mr. Chairman, in his remarks on Tuesday last he put it on the basis, and I read his speech very carefully, first of all of inflation. He says there is inflation arising out of the war just as there is out of every war. Then, his second piece of evidence was the quotation of certain remarks made by members on this side of the house with respect to housing conditions.
What has been said, Mr. Chairman, with respect to housing conditions, shows it is a fact that emergent conditions on a national scale do exist in regard to this matter. That is no ground, however, for the assertion that there is a general national emergency. Look where that leads us. The minister himself, in reply to a question by the member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher), has said that the
Transitional Measures Act existence of this national emergency does create this result, that it does transfer to parliament the power, not simply to do what we are being asked to do in the present resolution, but to do much more. Parliament can then do anything by way of invading the normal jurisdiction of the provinces over property and civil rights.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yes, that is what it amounts to, because if a national emergency exists then parliament has a right to do anything that is required to meet that national emergency.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question? If a national emergency does not exist, in my hon. friend's judgment has this house the right to deal with rental control?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have already made it clear, following the plain statement of my leader in this house on Wednesday, that an emergency does exist with respect to housing. A measure with respect to rent control is, therefore, one of the steps arising out of that national emergency with respect to housing. It would not, however, be competent for parliament or the minister to say that, since there is a national emergency with respect to housing, that gives parliament the right further to invade the normal jurisdiction of the provinces over property and civil rights.
May I remind the house that the provinces pass most of their statutes in the exercise of their jurisdiction over property and civil rights. It is the main source of jurisdiction in all provincial legislatures. The proposition the Minister of Justice has put before the house tonight is tantamount to this: By reason of the existence of a national emergency there exists in parliament today the right to trespass upon the provincial field of property and civil rights when parliament, by a majority of one if you please, deems necessary. Now, proclaim that broad principle throughout this country. The member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Lesage), instead of proclaiming his idle threats and threshing straw that was threshed out in this house three days ago, should go down to his constituency and proclaim the stand of the Minister of Justice in support of the proposition that there exists in this country such a national emergency as vests in the parliament of Canada the right to trespass completely on the provincial field of property and civil rights.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I have just received a challenge, and I will answer it. I will answer the member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) by

Transitional Measures Act quoting the words of Viscount Haldane. In so doing, I shall be in much better legal company than my friend the member for Eglinton with his imagination.
Their lordships, therefore, entertain no doubt that however the wording of sections 91 and 92 may have laid down a framework under which, as a general principle, the dominion parliament is to be excluded from trenching on property and civil rights in the provinces of Canada, yet in a sufficiently great emergency such as that arising out of war, there is implied the power to deal adequately with that emergency for the safety of the dominion as a whole.
That is quite different from what the member for Eglinton said.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is that the Fort Frances case?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yes, it is the Fort Frances Pulp and Power Company Limited case. Parliament has the power to deal with the emergency. It has to be a national emergency in order that the dominion may invade the field of property and civil rights. The extent of that emergency determines the extent to which the dominion can invade the field of property and civil rights. When the bill comes before the house, the extent to which we may, under the present emergency, invade the field of property and civil rights will be decided by this house. I understand that is the procedure. It seems to me we are wasting a lot of time discussing things that do not matter at this stage.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: We do not know yet what the bill will be.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question? I think the hon. gentleman will admit that the validity of the legislation must depend upon the emergency being a national emergency.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Oh, definitely, and I contended a few moments ago that there was a national emergency. The lack of housing is felt from Halifax to Vancouver, and that is a national emergency.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I was
involved in a debate such as this when this matter was brought before the house on an earlier occasion.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Louder.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I expressed my views at the time the omnibus bill came before this house. I should like to put myself on record in this session concerning the manner in which this proposal has been brought before the house. I have not changed my mind on the principle involved, but I have changed my mind concerning the procedure.
I am glad to see a new Minister of Justice, who is a real Canadian, dealing with these matters. He is not asking us to do this for

Britain as the former Minister of Justice did. I would say that, after the 27th of this month-

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Ha, ha.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Do not
laugh, my friends, because I would say this to you. If you continue your filibuster, you will have to take the responsibility if these emergency powers lapse. I know what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), "gorgeous George", said in Ontario last June, "Make Ontario Strong," and what Duplessis said in July, "Make a country of our province." If hon. members opposite go back to their ridings and say they would like to Balkanize this country instead of doing what we propose to do, namely, to make this country just as big and strong as the United States, I would say that some of them will never show up again.
When we come to this matter of emergency [DOT] powers, I would say that, if the Tory party wishes to take the responsibility of filibustering this emergency power legislation out of existence, thus bringing about the possibility of tenants-who constitute seventy-seven per cent of the people in Canada in the large cities-being thrown into the streets or with the prospect maybe of having an increase of two hundred or three hundred per cent in their rent, that is their responsibility. But I do not think it is a proper thing for the government to swing an election on this item. It would be the responsibility of the Tory party if all the tenants in this country were put on the sidewalks unless they accepted an increase of two hundred or three hundred per cent in their rents.
Then there is the question of margarine in certain places. We have these emergency powers to do certain things about agriculture. If the Tory party wishes to take the responsibility for increasing the price of butter and doing away with subsidies I would say, all right. I think it is about time that the Tory party showed its colours.
The new leader of the opposition conducted a sort of campaign against which I participated with the leader of the Liberal party in Ontario.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The Grit campaign.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Yes, the
Grit campaign; and I am not ashamed of it because it is the greatest thing a Canadian can do now.
Since the leader of the opposition has been here, he has been asking for provincial rights.
I should like to know why this man, with all his ostentation, has admitted that he would step down from being premier of a

province to become leader of the opposition at Ottawa; because if the provinces are on the top, why should he come down here?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: You will find out in a month or two.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
If these
emergency powers do not go through by March 27 by reason of the filibuster of the opposition, they will have to take the responsibility; the Tory party will have to take the responsibility. The Tory party will have put on the sidewalks all the beds of the tenants, who will have no more consideration because Ottawa will no longer protect them. Neither will Mr. Duplessis nor Mr. Kennedy any longer protect the small people. I say to hon. members opposite, if they want that, let them go to the people of Canada and say: What do you think? If we cannot go through with these emergency powers on account of the filibustering of the Tory organization, it is about time that this House of Commons was dissolved. We are in a position to say, "gentlemen, we are not afraid".

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Shall I report the resolution?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I have been up on my feet several times trying to catch the eye of the Chairman. I am glad I have it because it gives me a chance to say briefly that this debate seems to me to be a tremendous waste of time. All that we see happening is the same old shadow-boxing. Any member who cares to go back to the 1935 debates, when the Tories were in power, will find that they were putting up the same arguments then as the Liberals are putting up now and that the Liberals are putting up now the same arguments which the Tories were putting up then. There is very little reality in this entire debate.
As far as the Tories are concerned, their motto should be autre temps, autre moeurs, because I have here on page 4186 of Hansard of 1935 a statement by my friend the hon. member for Stanstead. A little while ago I think he said that the only emergency which really could arise was when the enemy was at the gate. He has changed his mind radically since 1935, for then he was of opinion that when the world was in a state of dislocation it might conceivably cause a national emergency. I do not like to be unfair to him but I shall quote him here when he was answering Mr. Rinfret, who was then the member for St. James. The member for St. James objected to the artificial methods which were being used by the Tory government, and the now hon. member for Stan-
Transitional Measures Act stead said in part-and 1 am trying to be completely fair in this quotation-as follows:
. . . but I believe the hon. member will admit that the whole world is in a state of dislocation.
The hon. member for Stanstead was then defending the Natural Products Marketing Act which the Liberals were attacking, of course, most savagely. The hon. gentleman went on to say:
There come times in the health of the individual as in that of a nation, when it is necessary that he have recourse to extraordinary means. Stimulants in times of crises are admitted by all to be not only wise but necessary.
Perhaps the hon. gentleman will admit that this is a time of crisis. Perhaps he will admit there is some international dislocation today and that therefore these measures we have in front of us, poor and attenuated as they may be, may within limits be wise and are certainly necessary. Then he went on later to say:
It has been necessary to resort during a period of disequilibrium to extraordinary methods.
That to some extent is precisely what is happening today, and I hope he will ask his colleagues to refer to those words which he spoke in 1935 and let us get on with the business of the house.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: We have been listening to a battery of legal experts on this question. They have been exceedingly interesting. The hon. member for Stanstead made one of the greatest addresses on this subject that we have heard in this house for some time. He pointed out very strongly that this parliament should pass many of its final decisions by guidance of the judiciary of this country. When I was a little boy my father used to say to me: "We have an appointed judiciary which is far superior to the courts of the United States, where many of them are elected." From time to time we hear people remarking that our courts are for the rich and not for the poor. It little behooves this government to set any example by not seriously considering the decisions of the Canadian courts, particularly the courts of appeal, when a court of appeal holds that there is no state of emergency.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: They all did not hold that.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Not as a member of parliament, but as a member of this house, and a representative of the people as well as the members of the legal profession, the labouring man, the grocer, the merchant or people of any other walk of life, I say that before we put a steam roller through the laws of this country, or a rubber stamp on those laws, simply because we belong to a party, we should reflect on what we do. As members of parliament and representatives of the

Transitional Measures Act people, we should reflect on the fact that an appeal court of Canada, comprised of men of substance and men whom we all hold in the highest regard, have stated that in their opinion there is no state of emergency. Let us not for one moment say that because we are the parliament of Canada we have a right over all the people, including appeal courts.
So far as getting on with the business of this country is concerned, let me say to the members of the C.C.F. party, who say that we have been holding a filibuster, that as long as I am in this House of Commons and I have an opinion I will voice it on behalf of the people whom I represent. Irrespective of flippant laughter I shall argue whether or not legislation going through the House of Commons is beneficial to all. At no time shall I try to stir up one class of people against another, as they do. I shall fight for the workingman, but I shall also fight for the other classes in this country. It is pretty near time they did a little of that instead of trying to antagonize and advocate class legislation as they do on almost every occasion when they rise to their feet in this House of Commons. They say that the poor workingman is going to be on the street because he cannot pay more rent. What about the landlord who owns a $10,000 house and is not getting more than $12 a month for it? Let us be a little fair about this question. There is no national emergency. The C.C.F. know that, but they want this parliament to rule as they rule in Russia. That is the true story. I hope I never bring my mentality to the low ebb that they do.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I do not propose to follow the speaker who has just taken his seat. There seems to be an accepted opinion in this house that a national emergency is the only reason why this parliament can legislate in such a way as to encroach upon section 92 of the British North America Act. I do not agree with that. A national emergency may be one reason; but according to the decision of the privy council in the Canada Temperance Act case, this parliament has also power to legislate upon any matter which, as the court says, by its inherent nature is of national importance, even though the matter legislated upon may touch upon the subjects contained in section 92 of the British North America Act. I think that is the situation here at least with some of these controls that we have under consideration.
There is the matter of price controls. I maintain that this parliament has power to legislate upon price control, whether there is an emergency or not. I think we agreed with that, and I think the hon. member for Stan-stead a few moments ago agreed that we in
Canada have power to legislate upon anything we want to. However, our legislative powers are divided between the dominion and the provinces.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Within the constitution.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Yes, that is right. Either we in this parliament, or the provincial legislatures, have power to legislate on price control. I do not think there is any doubt about that. Then evidence would be brought forward as to whether or not price control is a matter of provincial concern or national concern. I maintain, Mr. Chairman, that price control would be a matter of national concern because price control is unthinkable within the provinces themselves. Price control can only be enforced in an economic entity, and the whole of Canada, all the nine provinces, and ten after a week or so, are the economic entity. It is only within that economic entity that price control can be enforced. Therefore this parliament would have power to legislate upon it. Let me give an example. Recently, the supreme court held that the dairy act was ultra vires. With great respect to the majority of that court, I think the decision is wrong in law, and I think the chief justice was right in his decision, because later developments have proved it. If the decision were made now perhaps it would be made the other way.
The dairy act was enacted in order to give protection to the dairy farmers. It was a matter of price control, was it not? It was held to be ultra vires. The province of Quebec has now passed a similar law, and a very strict law I understand, in order to protect the dairy farmers of Quebec, in order to protect the price of butter in Quebec. Did it have that effect? No. The price of butter has gone down in Montreal, just as it has in Toronto and in Ottawa. Therefore, there is plain proof that the matter of price control of dairy products, the matter of price control of any other products, must rest within this dominion because the dominion as a whole is an economic entity. I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that as far as the law is concerned the Minister of Justice does not need to worry. I agree with him that this bill is clearly within the jurisdiction of this parliament.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
There is another question on which the house will wish to have some further information. The legislation of itself does not and cannot validly create a national emergency. The committee must be concerned as well about what steps are being taken to deal with the conditions which the government asserts constitute the condition of national emergency. I do not think enough time has been spent in this debate considering that aspect of the matter.

As things now stand the government is quite prepared to ask parliament for the vesting of these special and extraordinary powers, which normally repose in the provinces, so long as any case can be made out, to satisfy the majority across the way who support the government, that a national emergency exists.
It has been very hard to get out of the government any clear definition of what these national conditions are which constitute a national emergency. I mentioned earlier that we got from the Minister of Justice just two indications; one was inflation and the other was a shortage of houses. It is quite clear that we have inflation; it is equally clear that we have a grave shortage of housing. We apparently differ as to the powers that arise in that event. But I should like to know now, Mr. Chairman, just what the government is going to do to try to cure these conditions.
Let us concern ourselves for the moment with the conditions. Tonight we have had a legal argument. I should like the government now to make quite clear what it is going to do to bring to an end the national emergency which they say exists with respect to inflation and housing. It may be opportune to give the Minister of Justice a little rest for a while this evening, and to invite the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply to give the house some enlightenment with regard to this problem. It is obvious that housing conditions have entered largely into the thinking of the government-certainly they have entered largely into the reasons they have put forward tonight in arguing for the existence of a national emergency.
Will the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply give an indication to the house as to how far the government considers the emergency in housing extends today? We know that the president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation said not long ago that there was an emergent shortage today to the extent of 150,000 houses. That was the purely emergent shortage. I want to know what the government is going to do with regard to that emergent shortage, whether when the 150,000 houses are built the emergency will be ended, and-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I rise to a point of order. We are considering a resolution preceding a bill to continue certain controls which for some years now have been on the statute books. What is concerned now is the administration of these controls and not, I suggest, any of the matters to which the hon. member has been referring.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I cannot imagine anything more far-fetched than the minister's argument. Surely the only valid argument that can be put forward in support of maintaining
Transitional Measures Act rent control is that there is a shortage of housing, one which has reached critical, emergent and national proportions.
I want to know, and I think every member in the house wants to know, how long the emergency will be permitted to extend. Surely we are not going to be content simply to let the emergent condition continue, and to say that because of the existence of an emergent condition we will vest special powers in the government, or government boards. Surely it is the duty of every intelligent member of the House of Commons to seek to eliminate those conditions of shortage, and the condition of inflation. Surely that is our principal responsibility.
Before I am called upon on second reading of the bill to subscribe to giving the government special powers, I want to know what the government are going to do to cure and to eliminate the condition which they say has given rise to the existence of a condition of national emergency with respect to housing.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: On the point of order raised by the Minister of Justice, I am of the opinion that the hon. member could ask the government how long they think the emergency is likely to last. But at this time to raise the question as to what the government is going to do about these emergencies is, I think, beyond the powers of this committee. If that were done the government would have to give its plan with respect to housing, and whatever else may come up. The question of housing comes within another department entirely.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Surely, Mr. Chairman, it is not a question of departments, simply because the Minister of Justice has introduced this bill. Surely to goodness the whole basis of the continuance of rental control is the shortage of housing. You say it is proper to discuss the question as to how long the national emergency will continue? Very well; I am very much interested in the question as *o how long the national emergency will continue. I think it is perfectly fair to ask what we are doing and what we are going to do to try to speed up the elimination of the emergency. What are we going to do? What is the government going to do? What is it going to ask parliament to do with a view to shortening the time during which the emergent condition will be permitted to continue to prevail in Canada? That is a matter of prime importance, when we are in committee of the whole on a measure of this kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Speaking to the point of order -which I presume my hon. friend has been speaking to; otherwise he would be out of order-may I say it is one thing to allege a national emergency as the foundation for

Transitional Measures Act jurisdiction to pass this bill, as we are doing here, and it is another thing to take steps to cure it. When the bill comes down and the terms of it are seen, the period of time during which we are seeking these controls will be apparent. But surely, sir, we should not, certainly not at this stage, discuss the matter of housing, steel, poultry, butter, lettuce or citrus fruits-because, if we do, we will be here until Christmas.
What this measure is concerned with is the continuance, for a further period as yet undetermined but which will be disclosed when the bill is brought down, of the controls which we have had for the past several years. All of these matters to which the hon. member has referred might properly be the topic of discussion when departmental estimates are being considered. But certainly they are not properly discussed on the present occasion.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I think the minister will admit-

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Can anyone else, except a Tory, have a go in this House of Commons?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I think the hon. member will admit-

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Who has the floor?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I understand the hon.
member for Stanstead is about to speak to the point of order.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No, I was not.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Then I would rule that the matter of going into the question of the general policy of housing, and all the details with respect to housing, and the Central Mortgage Corporation, would not be in order at this time.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there has been a complete misapprehension of what I was trying to do. I was not going into details with respect to the administration of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
I did mention a statement by the chairman of that corporation in which he indicated the extent of the emergency which exists in housing in Canada today.
Now the minister says that when the bill comes down we will know exactly the period during which the government is asking for continuance of control. We have been told that already, with respect to rent control. They want to continue it for a year. But that is not an answer to my question. If it is said that there is a national emergency today, then I want to know what the government is doing to cure it. What is the government doing with respect to this question
[Mr. Garson. 3

of emergent conditions, and critical conditions with respect to housing?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I want to know if it is going to go on for a year. I want to know what is going to happen after that. It is perfectly proper to ask how long the emergency will last, and I am asking that question.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: "Order" -what do you mean?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The Chairman has given his ruling.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: You said earlier, Mr. Chairman, it was perfectly proper to ask how long the emergency was going to last.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: You will find it in the bill.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I want the government to say how long the emergency will last. I am asking them, further, to tell the committee what they are doing to shorten that period of time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The hon. member has asked the government to say how long the emergency will last. We are legislators; we are not prophets. There is an emergency, and this is one of the means of dealing with it. I submit, as I did before, that all my hon. friend's remarks at the present time are out of order; and I would ask for a ruling to that effect.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I would rule that the hon. member was in order when he asked the government how long the emergency would last. Whether or not the government can answer it, or desire to answer it, is another question. I would also rule that the question as to the details of what the government is doing in respect of the emergency is not in order at this time.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am content to leave it, Mr. Chairman, as the Minister of Justice has put it-if that is his answer-because he has said he is not prepared to hazard any conjecture whatsoever, or to give any statement to the house as to how long this emergency will last. As to my second question, which was what the government was doing about it, the minister's answer is nil. I am quite prepared to agree with that answer, that the government is doing nothing about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: My hon. friend knows quite well when he makes that statement that it is not a correct one because I have never said that we were doing nothing. What I did say was that my hon. friend's question was out of order.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: If the government have anything to say as to just what they are doing or propose to do to eliminate or shorten this period of emergency, let them say so now. If they have nothing to say, I say to them that they are doing nothing about these emergency conditions.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I have sat here all this week and listened to a torrent of words about nothing. I am about sick of all this stalling and fooling around.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: By whom?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Somebody across the way asks "by whom"? I do not think there is any doubt as to who is doing the fooling and the stalling. During, this week some forty hon. members have spoken on these particular questions, and thirty of them have been Tories. I do not think there is any doubt as to who is doing the stalling.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The only other observation I want to make in this debate is that I am as interested as any hon. member of this house in finding out what the bill contains. I am not prepared to indulge in a lot of shadowboxing at this stage. All that is asked in the resolution now before us is that we permit the introduction of that bill. When we come to second reading, if things are not in it that we think should be in it or things are in it that we thin]; should not be there, I believe that is the appropriate time to really criticize. But until we have the bill before us we are simply flogging a dead horse in carrying on this debate, which is precisely what my hon. friends to my right have been doing all week. Though we have only another hour to sit this week I do hope we may conduct ourselves as the people of the country expect this parliament to be conducted, and permit the bill to be introduced.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I do not think the Minister of Justice questions the fact that we are dealing with a matter which affects the constitution. He has stated in clear terms that the validity of the legislation to be founded upon this resolution depends upon the existence of an emergency. Here may I say that I was not speaking about an emergency in the interesting passage read to the committee a short time ago by the hon. member for Winnipeg North. He read from a speech I made in this house some years ago, when possibly my hair was more abundant and possibly not quite as white as it is

today. As the record shows, I was talking about the Natural Products Marketing Act, which was based not upon an emergency but, as the minister well knows, upon concurrent legislation in all the provinces, and upon the theory that this legislation of the nine provinces empowered this parliament to enact legislation it might not otherwise enact. On that issue, which was as remote from the question of an emergency as a camp meeting is from a beer garden, I expressed certain views, not one word of which I desire to retract at this time. What I said had no bearing upon the question of an emergency. As a distinguished member of the legal profession, Mr. Chairman, you will recollect that this matter of the constitutionality of the Natural Products Marketing Act went first to the Supreme Court of Canada and then to the privy council. There the legislation was held to be unfounded, not because there was no emergency-because emergency was not invoked as its basis-but because the provinces had not the power to enact legislation giving jurisdiction to this parliament.
I think it well to bring these matters to the attention of the committee, and even to the attention of the hon. member for Ontario. May I remind him that we have a constitution. We pride ourselves upon respecting it. We know that our liberties and the very essence of our well-being depend upon respect for the constitution. If there be no emergency, as the Minister of Justice admits, this parliament has no competency to pass the anticipated legislation.
Now I want to say just one word about the attitude of hon. gentlemen to my left and across the way who are sometimes pleased to call us Tories. What people are called does not matter very much. If the name be disrespectful, it may reflect upon the upbringing and good taste of them who use the language; but I have no complaint on that score. This is a serious question which goes to the very wellsprings of our national existence. If it be competent to this parliament to enact legislation of this kind in the absence of a national emergency, then Canada ceases to be a confederation and becomes a unitary state. I think we will all concede that the provinces would not have come into confederation, we would not have come into existence as a nation, otherwise than on the basis of confederation, with distinct rights, privileges and powers reserved to the separate entities, the provinces, that went to make it up. I hope I can discuss this matter quite dispassionately. I am willing to assume that every hon. gentleman in this house is interested in arriving at a conclusion which will respect the constitution.
Transitional Measures Act
There are a number of gentlemen on this side of the house, some of whom have spent a life that is beginning to be long, in the pursuit of the law. They are not infallible; but some people think they know something about their profession. They are putting forward a point of view that the Minister of Justice, although opposed to it, does not consider either futile or time-wasting. I think we shall make better progress and arrive at a saner and safer conclusion if gentlemen are permitted to express their views amid that attention which is characteristic of a deliberative legislative body.
The question is one of major importance. To style this discussion a waste of time is an expression of petulance or possibly, if one wished to be extremely kind, is a failure to understand all that is at issue. There has been criticism of those who have but put forward a point of view which has found repeated expression in the courts. Some people talk very lightly of the courts. Under the Canadian system of government, which is the system of the rule of law, Canadians depend upon the courts as the final arbiter, as the great check upon the legislative and administrative branches of government. The case in which the legislation was enacted, on which I was speaking when I uttered the passage quoted by the member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart), referred in no way to a national emergency. Consequently, the passage that he read has no bearing upon this present issue. I have asked the hon. minister to point to those conditions which create the national emergency which will justify the legislation.
The hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Lesage) has discussed the question in a very interesting way. Nevertheless, all of the judges of the court of appeal of Manitoba arrived at a unanimous decision that the law based upon an emergency was defective for lack of power. It is quite true that at least one of them did not find it necessary to pass upon the question of an emergency because the law was found invalid for other reasons. Nevertheless, it was not said that there was no emergency. At least two of the judges found in terms most categorical that there was no national emergency. We have the finding of the trial judge and we have the unanimous finding of the court of appeal confirming that judgment, with at least two, if not three, of the members of that bench finding that there was no emergency. That being the case, it seems to me-

Just a moment. We are now asked to suspend the constitution. The constitution is the agreement under which the provinces came together and under which we undertook to work out our difficulties and destiny; under which we undertook to colonize, civilize and redeem from the wilderness the vast areas of the northern sectors of this continent. Now, my friend may ask his question, and I thank him for waiting.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: My friend has given a very Seamed dissertation on the constitution. I want to ask him this simple question-one of the questioners requested a prophecy and I believe the Minister of Justice said he was not a prophet-

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It was the Minister of Agriculture who said that.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Just you keep quiet. I want to say this to my hon. friend. If wind could solve problems, there would not be any problems at all. I should like to ask this very simple question: Does the hon. member not think there would be an emergency if rent control fell by the wayside at the end of this month?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: If my hon. friend asks for a personal opinion, I am willing to give it, but I say that at the present time that is not the question before us.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: What is the question?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: If we are asked to declare that there is a national emergency which warrants the suspension of the constitution, my opinion for what it is worth, based upon such examination as I have been able to make of the facts and of the case law, is that there is not such an emergency.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I should like to tell the hon. member that this government is charged with the safety of the state. No doubt my learned friend is in the very fortunate position of owning a home and all the things necessary 

to make that home possible. I think he will agree with me that he would shudder to think what would happen in his home city of Montreal if rent control fell by the wayside. This is a practical problem and, in my judgment in simple English, it is a grave emergency facing this country.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has put his question fairly. My answer is this. If he feels there is something of such a nature so definite and dire that it requires the suspension of the constitution, then let him introduce ah act setting forth the situation and we will weigh it carefully and deal with it in consequence. It could then be debated here. Instead of that the government is offering an omnibus bill empowering it to carry on under arbitrary powers with a suspended constitution. It is attempting to perpetuate a type of administration which is a denial of the constitution and a denial of all the rights that are reserved both to individuals and to provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I wonder if the hon. gentleman will permit a question?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
