speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Would the hon. member agree with his own leader that the judgment in the Manitoba case to which he has been referring does not go so far as to declare that the transitional powers act is ultra vires?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I do not think that judgment had to go as far as that. I am suggesting here that the judgment said, among other things, that there was no power under the emergency transitional powers act to pass a certain order in council which permitted the government to take over Nolan's grain. That is the holding of the court. The court furthermore held that, there being no emergency, there was no power in the government to do what it had done. I am not at the moment going to argue, and I am not obliged to argue, that the act itself is invalid. But the order in council was invalid. I reiterate this suggestion. If hon. gentlemen feel that there is a certain condition which requires remedial legislation, let us deal with that situation. But do not ask us to pass an act which empowers the federal cabinet to occupy the whole field of legislation without regard to provincial and civil rights.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I too am one of those members who have sat in the house for some considerable time listening to this debate.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: How are your knees?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
With these Senate documents under my desk, my knees get sore. Before I say what I intend to say, I want to set the

minds of hon. members at rest with respect to the way in which I shall vote. I intend to vote for the measure, because I do not oppose the measure itself at this particular time of the country's history. I rise, however, in protest against those who are expressing themselves as desirous of getting on with the business of this house. That statement may sound rather paradoxical. I listened to one gentleman on the government side of the house tonight while he spent ten or fifteen minutes talking about a filibuster. I heard another gentleman on this side of the house quote from Hansard; and he was obliged to brush the dust from its pages when he turned away back so many years to pit the Tories against the Liberals and the Liberals against the Tories. I heard another gentleman who followed him give quite a dissertation, the theme of which was: let us get on with the business of the house. I suggest that the person who makes the remark "let us get on with the business of the house" is always in favour of the motion.
What is the business of the house? It is just as much the business of this house to prevent legislation from going through as it is to put it through. If a member or a party is vigorously and conscientiously opposed to a measure, and likewise if the government is as vigorous and conscientious in its desire for a measure to be passed, will you please tell me what conceivable method there is at the disposal of those who oppose the measure to prevent it from being passed? What conceivable method is there? I am not surprised at filibusters. Perhaps we should have more of them. I say that it is perfectly within the right of members of parliament to talk to their hearts' content on any measure that comes before us. I say that members of parliament are elected to this House of Commons to talk. There are only two things you can do when you sit in the chamber. You can either talk or keep silent. That is all there is to do. If you were not sent here to talk, what on earth were you sent here to do?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Listen.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I would say this to hon. members. Just go back to your constituencies, bid for the votes of your people, tell them, "If you vote for me I will go into the House of Commons; I will sit in my chair and I will never say a word." Tell them that, and see how far you will get.
With that in mind I simply say this. Every member in this house has a right to unburden his soul with respect to any measure that places a burden on it. Having said that, I am prepared to vote right now. But if anybody
Transitional Measures Act wants to talk, I am not prepared to say that he should not do so.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
For the last little while the debate, in my opinion, has not had much to do with the subject matter which is before us; and I hope that you will pardon me, Mr. Chairman, if I just continue in that strain for a moment. I do not agree with the hon. member for Macleod that members are sent to this house just to talk. Members are sent to this house to express their views on certain questions-as a matter of fact, on any question that may arise. But after they have presented their views, in my opinion they should not undertake to present the same views half a dozen times. The house has heard them once. We are sent here to enact legislation which may be beneficial to the people who sent us here. We may differ as to what the legislation is. When I rose to speak I was going to say that there is no man in this house to whom I like to listen more than I do to the hon. member for Stanstead. He was out of the chamber when I rose to speak, but I see that he is back now. I like to listen to his reasoned statements, whether I can agree with them or not.
I do not agree with what he said tonight that this is merely a matter of law. The law is important, but there can be no law until this parliament acts first. This parliament must pass the law. Then if some person is not satisfied with it, he can take it to the courts, and the courts will deal with it. But if this parliament is prevented from doing anything-and it very well may be prevented -there will be no use going to the courts after March 27 to find out if rent control is legal or illegal, because there will be no rent control. That is the question with which we are confronted at the moment.
Let me put it this way. The House of Commons is composed of a government and an opposition. The government, because it has the majority, is charged with the administration of the affairs of this country:	That
being the case, we have no right as an opposition, after we have stated our case, to prevent the government from doing what it considers right to do. We have a right to present our case as vigorously as we can. Then we should leave the matter to a vote of the house. But we have no moral right, in my opinion, to stand up here day after day and hold up the work that we were sent here to do for the people of Canada. We often in this house refer to the mother of parliaments. If this bill came before the house at Westminster, so many days would be allotted to debating it. After that was over, a vote would be taken.
I maintain that in a certain traditional and legal sense the opposition has the right to

Transitional Measures Act hold up the business of the house as long as we are foolish enough to hold it up. But in the rules of the house there is a provision to shut off debate. In the nineteen years I have been here I have never seen it invoked except on one occasion. The reason for that is that governments do not want to be put in the position where they have to choke off debate. However, a time will come when one of two things must be done. Either the government will have to apply closure or it will have to allow its legislation to lapse because it cannot get it through the house. If that is what my hon. friends want, it is their business of course, and they can settle it with the country.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
At this time I should like to make a statement with respect to the discussion that took place earlier today. I have looked into the question of quoting Senate debates on the floor of the House of Commons and I am now prepared to make a statement.
It is forbidden in the United Kingdom parliament to refer to debates in the House of Lords, which in turn does not allow reference to the debates of the House of Commons. We have no standing order on this rule of debate but the decisions of our Speakers and Deputy Speakers are unanimous in accepting the practice followed in the United Kingdom. The main object of this practice seems to be to prevent members of one house from answering members of the other house, thus bringing about a joint debate between the Senate and the House of Commons.
Is the rule so rigid that it prevents members from quoting under any circumstances extracts from debates which took place in the distant past or does it apply only to speeches recently delivered in the Senate? A reasonable view has to be taken in this matter. Our authorities make no distinction between the dates on which the speeches were delivered, but in the United Kingdom the rule applies only to recent speeches. On December 16, 1902, when Sir William Har-court attempted to quote a speech delivered by a minister in the House of Lords, he was stopped by Mr. Speaker Court-Gully, who said:
Order, order! The right honourable gentleman began oy saying he would read a speech made in the House of Lords. I must remind him that it is not in order to quote from recent debates in the house. I have no doubt that the right honourable gentleman will be able to state what he understands to be the views of the government as expressed in the House of Lords without quoting the speeches.


I suggest that we ought to follow the same practice as at Westminster.
The great difficulty is to decide what may be called a recent debate in the Senate. As to the current session there can be no doubt; but how far back must a speech have been delivered for it to be considered old enough to be allowed to be quoted in the House of Commons? This ought to be decided according to circumstances.
If the House of Commons is considering a measure passed in the Senate a few years ago and likely to come up again during the current session, it seems to me that, in such a case, if members of this house quoted the debates of the Senate, they might start an unpleasant controversy between the two houses. But I see no reason to debar members from quoting parts of speeches delivered in the Senate many years ago on questions which do not then call for an immediate decision of the house. What we want to avoid is a discussion between the two houses of parliament. There is nothing better calculated to bring a conflict between the Senate and the Commons than having members of the one attacking the members of the other on the floors of their respective chambers.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Garson thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 86, to amend the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act, 1947.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

This brings me to a close. I simply wanted to place before the minister the feeling of uncertainty which I know does exist among the poultrymen of Vancouver island. They are perturbed about the loss of markets and the threat which they feel exists to the continuity of their business.

North Atlantic Treaty Proposed for Signature During the First Week in April, 1949
Preamble
The parties to this treaty reaffirm their faith in the purposes and principles of the charter of the United Nations and their desire to live in peace with all peoples and all governments.
They are determined to safeguard the freedom, common heritage and civilization of their peoples, founded on the principles of democracy, individual liberty and the rule of law.
They seek to promote stability and wellbeing in the north Atlantic area.
They are resolved to unite their efforts for collective defence and for the preservation of peace and security.
They therefore agree to this North Atlantic treaty:
Article 1
The parties undertake, as set forth in the charter of the United Nations, to settle any international disputes in which they may be involved by peaceful means in such a manner that international peace and security, and justice, are not endangered, and to refrain in their international relations from the threat or use of force in any manner inconsistent with the purposes of the United Nations.
Article 2
The parties will contribute toward the further development of peaceful and friendly international relations by strengthening their free institutions, by bringing about a better understanding of the principles upon which these institutions are founded, and by promoting conditions of stability and well-being. They will seek to eliminate conflict in their international economic policies and will encourage economic collaboration between any or all of them.
Article 3
In order more effectively to achieve the objectives of this treaty, the parties, separately and jointly, by means of continuous and effective self-help and mutual aid, will
maintain and develop their individual and collective capacity to resist armed attack.
Article 4
The parties will consult together whenever, in the opinion of any of them, the territorial integrity, political independence or security of any of the parties is threatened.
Article 5
The parties agree that an armed attack against one or more of them in Europe or North America shall be considered an attack against them all; and consequently they agree that, if such an armed attack occurs, each of them, in exercise of the right of individual or collective self-defence recognized by article 51 of the charter of the United Nations, will assist the party or parties so attacked by taking forthwith, individually and in concert with the other parties, such action as it deems necessary, including the use of armed force, to restore and maintain the security of the north Atlantic area.
Any such armed attack and all measures taken as a result thereof shall immediately be reported to the security council. Such measures shall be terminated when the security council has taken the measures necessary to restore and maintain international peace and security.
Article 6
For the purpose of article 5 an armed attack on one or more of the parties is deemed to include an armed attack on the territory of any of the parties in Europe or North America, on the Algerian departments of France, on the occupation forces of any party in Europe, on the islands under the jurisdiction of any party in the north Atlantic area north of the Tropic of Cancer or on the vessels or aircraft in this area of any of the parties.
Article 7
This treaty does not affect, and shall not be interpreted as affecting, in any way the rights and obligations under the charter of

Article 8
Each party declares that none of the international engagements now in force between it and any other of the parties or any third state is in conflict with the provisions of this treaty, and undertakes not to enter into any international engagement in conflict with this treaty.
Article 9
The parties hereby establish a council, on which each of them shall be represented, to consider matters concerning the implementation of this treaty. The council shall be so organized as to be able to meet promptly at any time. The council shall set up such subsidiary bodies as may be necessary; in particular it shall establish immediately a defence committee which shall recommend measures for the implementation of articles 3 and 5.
Article 10
The parties may, by unanimous agreement, invite any other European state in a position to further the principles of this treaty and to contribute to the security of the north Atlantic area to accede to this treaty. Any state so invited may become a party to the treaty by depositing its instrument of accession with the government of the United States of America. The government of the United States of America will inform each of the parties of the deposit of each such instrument of accession.
Article 11
This treaty shall be ratified and its provisions carried out by the parties in accordance with their respective constitutional processes. The instruments of ratification shall be
deposited as soon as possible with the government of the United States of America, which will notify all the other signatories of each deposit. The treaty shall enter into force between the states which have ratified it as soon as the ratifications of the majority of the signatories, including the ratifications of Belgium, Canada, France, Luxembourg, The Netherlands, the United Kingdom and the United States, have been deposited and shall come into effect with respect to other states on the date of the deposit of their ratifications.
Article 12
After the treaty has been in force for ten years, or at any time thereafter, the parties shall, if any of them so requests, consult together for the purpose of reviewing the treaty, having regard for the factors then affecting peace and security in the north Atlantic area, including the development of universal as well as regional arrangements under the charter of the United Nations for the maintenance of international peace and security.
Article 13
After the treaty has been in force for twenty years, any party may cease to be a party one year after its notice of denunciation has been given to the government of the United States of America, which will inform the governments of the other parties of the deposit of each notice of denunciation.
Article 14
This treaty, of which the English and French texts are equally authentic, shall be deposited in the archives of the government of the United States of America. Duly certified copies thereof will be transmitted by that government to the governments of the other signatories.
In witness whereof, the undersigned plenipotentiaries have signed this treaty. Done at Washington, the	day of April, 1949.
